3.title: Suffering for Righteousness: Wives, Husbands, and Christ's Victory
3.overview: Chapter 3 completes the household instructions for wives and husbands (vv. 1–7), calls the whole church to repay evil with blessing and to give a gentle reason for its hope (vv. 8–17), and grounds everything in Christ (vv. 18–22): his once-for-all death, his resurrection and his ascension to God’s right hand. The movement is from the household to the cosmos, and Christ’s victory over every power is the ground for enduring any unjust suffering.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The household instructions end with wives and husbands, both under the same Christ-pattern. The hard case Peter has in mind is a believing wife with an unbelieving husband, and the husband’s one verse is the heaviest.
verseByVerse.theology:
Reading This Passage Rightly

The Christ-pattern applies to wives and husbands alike. A believing wife may win an unbelieving husband by her conduct; a husband must honour his wife as a fellow heir of the grace of life.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A woman converted without her husband was in a precarious position.

Now: This is a text about witness in marriage, never about tolerating abuse.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, wives, be subject to your own husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives, when they see your respectful and pure conduct.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Peter 3 continues the theme of godly submission and suffering. Wives are to submit to their husbands, so that unbelieving husbands may be won by their lives rather than by words, adorned with the inner beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, like Sarah (vv. 1–6). Husbands are to live with their wives with understanding and honour, as co-heirs of grace (v. 7). All are to be united and tender, repaying evil with blessing (vv. 8–12). If they suffer for doing right, they are blessed; they honour Christ as Lord and are ready to explain their hope gently (vv. 13–17). For Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God; made alive in the Spirit, he proclaimed to the spirits in prison from Noah’s day (vv. 18–20). Baptism now saves, not by washing the body, but as the appeal of a good conscience to God, through the resurrection of Christ, who reigns over all powers (vv. 21–22).

Likewise, wives. Likewise, homoiōs, in the same way, ties this to what precedes, and that matters for reading it rightly. Peter has just described Christ, who did not revile in return and kept entrusting himself to the just Judge (2:23). What follows is that pattern applied: first to citizens (2:13), then to slaves (2:18), now to wives, and in verse 7 to husbands. Nobody in the household is exempt. Be subject, hypotassomenai, is the ordering word Peter used of citizens and the state, and will use of the whole congregation towards its elders and one another (5:5). It describes a voluntary, respectful following of a husband’s lead (Ephesians 5:22–24; Colossians 3:18; Titus 2:5). It is not a claim about worth; verse 7 will call her a fellow heir. And it is not submission to men in general. Your own husbands, tois idiois andrasin: one’s own husband, and no one else.

If some do not obey the word. Peter addresses the hard case. Do not obey the word, apeithousin tō logō, means they disbelieve the gospel. In that world a wife was expected to take her husband’s gods; Plutarch advised that a wife should worship only the gods her husband believed in and shut the door to strange rites. A woman who had become a Christian alone had done something socially outrageous and was in a genuinely precarious position: under Roman custom the children belonged to the father, and a husband could divorce her and keep them.

Without a word. The purpose is evangelistic. Won, kerdēthēsontai, means gained, won over, the term Paul uses for winning converts (1 Corinthians 9:19–22). The aim is her husband’s conversion. Peter is giving a woman with little power a strategy that might actually save the man she is married to. Without a word, aneu logou, is the striking phrase, and it is realistic. The gospel word has probably already been heard and rejected; she has likely said it, and saying it again and again will not help. Nagging, preaching at the dinner table and leaving tracts on his pillow will only harden him. What is left is the silent sermon of a godly life: the thing he cannot argue with. And this is the likewise at work. The Lord who won these women was the one who, when reviled, did not revile in return (2:23), and who stood silent before his accusers like a sheep before its shearers (Isaiah 53:7). A wife’s patient conduct in a hostile home is a copy of his, traced in a kitchen.

Respectful and pure conduct. See, epopteusantes, is the word from 2:12: observe closely, watch over time. A life observed daily at close quarters over years. Respectful, en phobō, is literally in fear: reverence towards God, which shows itself in respect for her husband. Pure, hagnēn, is chaste, holy. A husband who is watching for hypocrisy finds a wife who is kinder than before, more honest, more faithful, more joyful, and who does not despise him. Over time that is very hard to resist. Augustine’s mother Monica, married to a hot-tempered pagan, Patricius, won him to Christ before his death by exactly this, as her son records in his Confessions.

Where Christians differ: does wifely submission belong only to ancient culture? Egalitarians argue that Peter is giving missionary advice suited to a patriarchal culture, and that mutual submission without distinct roles is the Christian ideal today. Many who hold this view are faithful, Bible-believing Christians moved by real concern for women’s dignity, and they deserve to be heard as brothers and sisters. This commentary’s view: Peter’s concern is indeed partly missional, but he grounds the instruction in the example of holy women of the Old Testament (v. 5), and Paul grounds it in Christ and the church and in creation (Ephesians 5:22–33; 1 Corinthians 11:8–9). The complementarian view holds that husband and wife are equal in worth and co-heirs of grace (v. 7), with distinct roles: the husband leads with sacrificial love, the wife follows with respect and strength. Submission never requires sin (Acts 5:29), never makes the wife inferior, and never means enduring abuse: abuse is never to be tolerated, and a wife who is being abused should seek safety at once, with the church’s help. This commentary holds the complementarian view because the reasons Peter and Paul give reach back before any one culture, to creation and to Christ, while gladly admitting that godly Christians weigh those reasons differently.

Does this apply to all Christian wives, or only those with unbelieving husbands? It is the pattern for all wives, as Paul also teaches (Ephesians 5:22–24; Colossians 3:18), and Peter points to the holy women of old (v. 5); here he applies it to the hard case of an unbelieving husband. Submission is given to a husband in his rightful role, as to the Lord. It never means obeying a command to sin (Acts 5:29), and it never requires a wife to endure abuse; she may seek safety and help from the church and the law.

This is not a text about tolerating abuse. Peter is describing witness within a marriage, not endurance of violence; the same letter tells husbands their prayers will be blocked if they mistreat their wives. Anyone using verse 1 to keep a woman in danger is using it against its own author. Headship in Scripture is never a licence to dominate; it is the call to lay down one’s life, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). A man who uses his wife’s submission as a weapon has abandoned the very pattern that makes her submission possible.

What does submission actually look like in an ordinary Christian marriage? It looks like a wife who respects her husband in what she says to him and about him, supports his leadership rather than undermining it, and is willing to let him make the final decision when the two of them, having talked and prayed, still disagree. It does not mean she has no opinions, no voice or no gifts; the wife of Proverbs 31 runs a business and speaks with wisdom. It does not mean she obeys every man, or that she must stay silent about sin. And it is never one-sided: her husband is called to love her as Christ loved the church, which is a far heavier burden. Submission is a free gift, given to the Lord, through a husband.

I am married to an unbeliever and it has been many years. Should I give up hope? No. Peter gives this word precisely because the wait can be long. Keep praying; keep loving; keep living the gospel in front of him. You are not responsible for his conversion, which is God’s work, but you may be the means God uses, and many husbands have come to Christ after decades. Find support in your church; you were never meant to carry this alone. And remember that your faithfulness is precious in God’s sight now, whether or not you see the outcome. Paul says the unbelieving husband is in some sense made holy because of his wife (1 Corinthians 7:14), and that you do not know whether you will save him (7:16): there is room for hope.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not let your adorning be external—the braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear— but let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not let your adorning be external. Adorning, kosmos, means ornament, decoration, arrangement, and our word cosmetic comes from it. External, exōthen, means outward. Peter is not saying a woman should not care how she looks. He is speaking of where a woman’s adorning is located: what she is counting on to make her worth looking at.

Braiding, gold, clothing. Three items are named, and they were the recognised display of a wealthy Roman woman. Fashionable women wore elaborate hairstyles, sometimes woven with gold and pearls, which took time and a slave to arrange; the portrait busts of the period show it. Jewellery and expensive clothing displayed status, as in 1 Timothy 2:9. He is warning against making appearance the main thing.

The hidden person of the heart. The hidden person of the heart, ho kryptos tēs kardias anthrōpos, is the inner self, character, who you really are when no one is looking. The contrast is outer and visible against inner and hidden, and Peter does not tell her to stop adorning herself. He tells her to move the adornment. The pull Peter is resisting is not only a Roman one. Whenever we look to our appearance to make us acceptable, to be noticed, admired or envied, the mirror has become a judge whose verdict we live for, and it is a judge that always finds fault in the end. The gospel gives a verdict that does not wrinkle: accepted in Christ (Ephesians 1:6).

A gentle and quiet spirit. That word imperishable, aphthartos, again: the inheritance (1:4), the seed (1:23), and now this. Peter keeps setting one thing beside everything that decays, and hair and gold and cloth all belong to the perishing side. Outward beauty fades; inner beauty lasts for ever. Gentle and quiet needs rescuing from a caricature. Gentle is praus: meek, mild, a word Greek writers could use of a tamed animal, strength under control, and the word the Lord uses of himself: I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29). Quiet, hēsychios, means settled, tranquil, not agitated or anxious. Neither word means timid, silent or without opinions. Not a personality type, quiet versus loud, but a heart at rest in God. A noisy, laughing, talkative woman can have a quiet spirit; a silent one can be seething.

A composure that does not depend on circumstances. And it is a description of exactly what such a woman most needed. A Christian wife in a hostile household, unable to argue and unable to leave, is offered composure that does not depend on her circumstances improving. Gentleness and quietness are not weakness; they are what fear and anger look like when they have been handed over to God.

Very precious. There is the point of the whole paragraph. Very precious, polytelēs, very costly, is the word used of the expensive perfume poured on Jesus’ head (Mark 14:3). She is in a house where she is not valued and a society that valued the braided hair; Peter tells her what she looks like from the one perspective that will still be there in a thousand years. And Peter has already called Christ himself precious in God’s sight (2:4), though with a different Greek word. God values inner beauty more than all the jewellery in the world.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid braided hair, jewellery or nice clothes entirely; otherwise it would forbid the clothing you wear too. It forbids making outward appearance the main focus. Nor does it apply only to women; men too should be adorned with gentleness.

Is it wrong to care about how I look? No. God made beauty, and caring for your appearance in a way that is modest, appropriate and not extravagant honours him. The danger is when appearance becomes the place you look for your worth, the thing that consumes your time, money and thoughts, or a way of competing with others. Ask: how much of my time and money goes on the outside, and how much on the hidden person of the heart? Am I more anxious about a bad hair day than about an unkind word I spoke? The aim is not to neglect the body but to put it in its place.

How does someone become gentle and quiet in spirit? Not by suppressing your personality, but by bringing your fears and frustrations to God until they lose their grip. A quiet spirit grows from trust: the more you are convinced that God is in control and loves you, the less you need to fight, control or worry. Spend time in his presence. Bring him your anxieties specifically (5:7). Learn from Christ, who called himself gentle and lowly. And when you notice agitation rising, a sharp word, a need to have the last word, take it as a signal to pray rather than to push.

On a Tuesday. Notice who in your church has the beauty Peter describes. Often it is an elderly woman nobody would put on a magazine cover. Tell her.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is how the holy women who hoped in God used to adorn themselves, by submitting to their own husbands, as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. And you are her children, if you do good and do not fear anything that is frightening.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The holy women. Peter appeals to precedent. Holy women: the godly women of the Old Testament, like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Leah, Hannah, Ruth. And note the phrase he uses of them: they hoped in God. That is the source of the composure just described. These were not naturally placid women; they were women whose expectation was fixed somewhere secure. Their hope was not in their husbands or their beauty but in God, and that gave them the security to submit.

By submitting to their own husbands. Their adornment was a godly submission flowing from hope in God. It was not resignation, and it was not fear; it was the confident trust of women who knew who was really in charge of their lives.

Calling him lord. The reference is to Genesis 18:12, where Sarah, told she will have a son at ninety, laughs to herself and refers to her husband as my lord. Lord, kyrios, master, sir, was the ordinary courteous term of that world. Even in her private thoughts, she spoke of him with respect. Sarah is a surprising example, and that helps rather than hurts. She laughed at God’s promise; she gave Hagar to Abraham and then dealt harshly with her (Genesis 16:5–6; 21:10); she was not a model of quiet submission throughout. She was strong-willed and spoke frankly, and on one occasion God told Abraham to listen to her: whatever Sarah says to you, do as she tells you (Genesis 21:12). She was no doormat. Peter is not holding up a flawless woman but pointing to one whose hope was in God despite everything, which is precisely the encouragement a struggling wife needs.

Sarah’s journey. Think what Sarah’s hope cost her. She left her home in Ur and then Haran with a husband following a God she could not see, to a land she did not know. She lived in tents for decades. Twice Abraham passed her off as his sister to save his own skin, and twice God protected her (Genesis 12; 20). She waited twenty-five years for a promised son. Her submission was not to a perfect man; it was to an imperfect one, trusting a perfect God. And God honoured her: she is named in Hebrews 11 among the heroes of faith (Hebrews 11:11, though some translations make Abraham the subject of that verse), the mother of the promised line.

And you are her children. Children, tekna, here daughters. The same move Peter has made all through the letter: Gentile believers are given Israel’s ancestry. As believers are Abraham’s children by faith (Galatians 3:7), Christian women become Sarah’s daughters by following her example of faith. A former pagan wife in Cappadocia, with no Jewish blood at all, is told she belongs in the family of the mother of Israel.

Children of the free woman. Sarah matters because of the son she bore. Isaac, whose name means he laughs, was born when it was impossible, by God’s promise alone, and through his line came the Christ. Paul reads Sarah the same way: believers are children of the free woman, children of promise like Isaac, not children of the slave (Galatians 4:28–31). So to be Sarah’s daughter is more than to copy her manners. It is to share her son’s kind of birth, by promise and not by human strength, which is exactly what Peter said of his readers at the start: born again of imperishable seed (1:23). Every one of Sarah’s daughters is a miracle child of the Messiah who came from her line.

Do not fear. The second half of the condition is the surprise. Do good, agathopoiousai; fear, phoboumenai, be afraid; frightening, ptoēsis, terror, intimidation, alarm. That is not what we expect after a paragraph on gentleness and quietness. Peter’s picture of a godly wife ends in courage. The Greek echoes Proverbs 3:25: do not be afraid of sudden terror. Christian wives with pagan husbands faced real threats. Her composure is not fragility; she is not gentle because she is afraid. A woman who has hoped in God can be quiet in a hostile house precisely because there is nothing left in it that frightens her, including her husband’s anger.

What if my husband frightens me? Then Peter’s words, do not fear anything that is frightening, are a call to trust God, not to stay in danger. If your husband threatens, hits, controls or terrifies you, that is abuse, and God hates it. Submission never requires you to endure it, and you should not keep it secret. Tell a trusted friend and your pastor or elders, and if you are in danger, contact the police or an abuse helpline and get to a safe place. A godly church will support and protect you, and will call your husband to repentance. Seeking safety is not a failure of faith or of submission; it is what the courage Peter describes may look like.

For worship. The God of Sarah keeps his promises to women who laugh in disbelief. At her tent door he asked, is anything too hard for the LORD? (Genesis 18:14), and two thousand years later his angel gave the answer to a girl in Nazareth: nothing will be impossible with God (Luke 1:37). He has never failed a woman who hoped in him. He sees the wife in the hostile home, the widow, the woman waiting for decades; he counts her tears and names her among his heroes. And the Son of his impossible promises has overcome the world, so his daughters need fear nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, since they are heirs with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, husbands. The same word that opened the paragraph to wives, homoiōs, and it puts the man under the same Christ-pattern. In a culture where a husband’s authority was largely unquestioned, the mere existence of a command to him is remarkable. Peter gives him one verse to the wives’ six, which is not a measure of importance but of who most needed the encouragement, perhaps because fewer husbands in these congregations were believers, or because the wives were in the harder place. But the one verse is very heavy.

In an understanding way. Live with, synoikountes, means dwell together, share a home, and it includes the whole of married life, the sexual relationship among it. In an understanding way is literally according to knowledge, kata gnōsin. It requires him to know her: to have studied this particular woman well enough to live with her intelligently, her needs, her feelings, her fears and concerns, her gifts and her burdens. That is a lifetime’s work and it cannot be done at a distance, which rules out the husband who is present in the house and absent from the marriage.

The weaker vessel. Showing honour, aponemontes timēn, means assigning honour, paying respect, giving her what is her due. The phrase weaker vessel, asthenesterō skeuei, has been misused and needs stating carefully. Vessel is used of both of them, God’s containers (2 Timothy 2:21): she is the weaker of two vessels, so he is a vessel too. Weaker most likely refers to physical strength, and perhaps to social vulnerability in a world where women had few rights. Not weaker morally, intellectually or spiritually. And see what Peter does with it. The weakness is given as the reason for honour, not for contempt or command. Precisely because she is more vulnerable to him, he owes her more deference. That inverts the ordinary logic of power completely. Husbands must not exploit their greater strength, but use it to protect and honour, as a man handles fine porcelain with care, not because it is worth less than an iron pot but because it is worth more.

Heirs with you. Fellow heirs, synklēronomois, co-heirs, joint heirs: equal standing, equal inheritance, the same imperishable estate of 1:4. Spiritually, husband and wife are completely equal before God, inheriting the same eternal life (Galatians 3:28). Whatever verse 1 means, it cannot mean she is worth less, and Peter has settled that inside the same paragraph. Distinction of roles does not mean distinction of worth. One day he will stand beside her before the throne, and their welcome there will rest on the same grace, not on which of them was the head of the house.

A bruised reed he will not break. The husband’s likewise points him to the same Christ the wives were given (2:21–24), and it is the Christ of strength used for the weak. Matthew applies Isaiah’s words to him: a bruised reed he will not break, and a smouldering wick he will not quench (Matthew 12:20). He had all power, and he spent it touching lepers, lifting a woman bent double for eighteen years, defending a weeping woman at a Pharisee’s table, and speaking to his own mother from the cross to see her cared for. A husband who uses his strength to honour the more vulnerable is not being soft. He is tracing his Lord.

Prayers not hindered. Hindered, enkoptesthai, means cut in on, blocked, obstructed, as a road is blocked by a fallen tree or a trench dug across it. A man who treats his wife badly will find his prayer life obstructed. God takes her side against him, and will not carry on ordinary dealings with a man who is mistreating a fellow heir (Malachi 2:13–16). Relationship with God and relationship with one’s wife are bound together. A husband cannot be a lion of prayer in the church and a bully in the kitchen.

What does it mean for a husband to lead? To go first in love, in sacrifice and in serving. Christ’s headship over the church is the pattern, and he led by washing feet and dying (Ephesians 5:25–29). A Christian husband leads by praying with and for his wife, by taking responsibility for the spiritual health of the home, by listening carefully before deciding, by protecting her, and by putting her good before his own comfort. He does not make every decision, does not demand his way, and never uses his strength to frighten her. Do not be harsh with them (Colossians 3:19). Leadership that does not look like Christ is not biblical headship, whatever it calls itself.

How do I live with my wife in an understanding way if I do not understand her? Start by admitting it, and asking. Ask her what she needs from you, what burdens her, what makes her feel loved and what makes her feel dismissed, and then listen without defending yourself. Notice her moods and ask about them. Learn what her days are really like. Pray for wisdom (James 1:5). Understanding is not a gift some men have and others lack; it is knowledge gained by attention over years. The husband who keeps asking, keeps listening and keeps adjusting is obeying this verse, even if he still finds her a mystery.

On a Tuesday. If your prayers feel blocked, ask honestly whether there is something between you and your wife that needs putting right first. Apologise without excuses.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter turns to the whole church: how it treats its own members, and how it answers those who slander it. The answer is blessing instead of retaliation, and a hope visible enough to be asked about.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Forgotten Half of Verse 15

Repay evil with blessing. Be ready to give a reason for your hope, and give it with gentleness and respect.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Slandered believers were told to fear the Lord, not their accusers.

Now: A life that raises questions, and answers them courteously, is the best reply to slander.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, all of you, have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, a tender heart, and a humble mind. Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary, bless, for to this you were called, that you may obtain a blessing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally, all of you. Finally, to telos, in summary. The household instructions end and the whole congregation is addressed: citizens, slaves, wives, husbands, everyone. Five qualities follow, and they are all relational. Peter has been speaking about how believers live under pressure from outside; now he turns to how they live with one another, because a church under fire that turns on itself has already lost.

Have unity of mind. Unity of mind, homophrones, is like-mindedness, thinking together. Not uniformity of opinion on every question but a shared outlook on what matters most (Philippians 2:2): the same Lord, the same gospel, the same hope, the same direction.

Sympathy. Sympathy, sympatheis, is literally suffering-with, and it is the root of our word: feeling what the other feels. Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15). In a persecuted network of congregations that was not sentiment but survival. When one member was fined or beaten, the others felt it.

Brotherly love. Brotherly love, philadelphoi: loving as family. Peter has used the word before (1:22). The church is not a club of the like-minded but a family of the born-again, and families are where you learn to love people you did not choose.

A tender heart. A tender heart, eusplanchnoi, is literally having good inner parts. It is the gut-word, from the same root as the visceral term the Gospels use when Jesus saw the crowds and was moved with compassion (Matthew 9:36). Deep, felt kindness (Ephesians 4:32), not a professional politeness.

And a humble mind. Humble, tapeinophrones, lowly-minded: not thinking too highly of oneself (Philippians 2:3). It is a virtue the Bible largely taught the world, for in classical Greek the root was mostly an insult; it meant mean, abject, servile. It took the Son of God washing feet to make humility beautiful.

Do not repay. Then the command that everything has been building towards. Repay, apodidontes, means give back. It is not only violence that is forbidden but the returned insult, which is the retaliation actually available to people with no power, and therefore the one they would actually use. Do not retaliate in deed or word, as Christ did not (2:23; Romans 12:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:15).

But on the contrary, bless. Not merely refrain. Bless, eulogountes, means speak well of, and ask God’s good on, the very people slandering you: not neutrality but active good. It is the Lord’s own command: bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you (Luke 6:28; Romans 12:14). And Peter had heard it. No one blesses a slanderer by temperament; the Spirit of the Christ who blessed his enemies now lives in his people to make it possible (Galatians 5:22–23).

Obtain a blessing. The called-to language again from 2:21, eklēthēte. Obtain, klēronomēsēte, means inherit: the same family as the inheritance of 1:4. And the last clause is not a bargain, bless in order to be paid, but a description of the economy they are now in. They were called to inherit blessing, and blessing is therefore what they have to give away. You hand on what you were given. Those who bless show that they have been blessed, and they will inherit the blessing in full.

How can I bless someone who has hurt me badly? Begin with prayer, not feeling. Ask God to do them good: to bring them to repentance, to save them, to give them what they truly need. You can pray that honestly long before you feel warmly. Then refuse to curse them in your speech: no mocking, no running them down to others. When an opportunity comes to do them a kindness, take it, if it is safe. Blessing does not mean pretending the wrong did not happen, restoring trust that has not been earned, or putting yourself back in harm’s way. It means refusing to return the poison, and handing the case to God.

What about the person in church I simply do not get on with? Then the five words of verse 8 are your homework. Like-minded: focus on the gospel you share, not the preferences you do not. Sympathetic: find out what they are carrying. Brotherly: remember they are family by God’s choice. Tender: ask God to give you compassion for them. Humble: consider that they may find you hard work too. You do not have to become best friends. You do have to love them, speak well of them, and refuse to build a faction against them.

verseByVerse.quote: For "Whoever desires to love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit; let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it. For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love life and see good days. Peter supports the command with Psalm 34:12–16, and the choice is not accidental. He has already quoted this psalm in 2:3, and it is the psalm David wrote after escaping from Achish, king of Gath (called Abimelech in the psalm’s title), by pretending to be insane, scrabbling at the doors and letting spit run down his beard (Psalm 34 title; 1 Samuel 21:10–15). A man in real danger, with no power, getting out alive. It is a psalm of God’s protection of the persecuted righteous, and the right psalm for these readers. Love life and good days mean a blessed life, now and for ever. The offer is put as an invitation to ordinary human longing. Peter is not sneering at the wish for a good life; he is telling them where it is found.

Keep his tongue. The first instruction is about the mouth. He has just forbidden reviling in return (v. 9), and the psalm’s first counsel to a man in danger is the same: control what you say when they come at you. No reviling, no lies. Most of the damage we do to others, and to ourselves, comes out through the lips.

Turn away and do good. Both halves, and in that order. Avoidance and then action, which is the pattern the New Testament keeps: put off, and put on. A life of mere avoidance is empty; a life of good deeds that never turns from evil is hypocrisy.

Seek peace. The second verb is the hunting word: chase it down. Peace here is not passivity; it is something you go after, and it will not be found by waiting for it to arrive (Romans 12:18; Hebrews 12:14). Peacemakers are not people who avoid conflict, but people who run towards broken relationships to mend them.

The eyes of the Lord. Then the ground, and it is the reason any of this is possible. Two organs of attention. He is watching, and he is listening, which is precisely what a slandered congregation could not be sure of. The persecuted are not forgotten.

The face of the Lord. Peter includes the hard half, and it belongs. God opposes evildoers. The reason a Christian can decline to return the insult is not that the insult does not matter. It is that it has been noticed by someone better placed to deal with it: the same argument as 2:23, where Christ handed the case to the one who judges justly. And Peter stops the quotation before the psalm’s next line, which speaks of cutting off the memory of them from the earth, perhaps leaving room for persecutors to repent.

The righteous man of Psalm 34. The psalm Peter quotes goes on: many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him out of them all. He keeps all his bones; not one of them is broken (Psalm 34:19–20). John saw that promise kept at Golgotha, when the soldiers broke the legs of the two criminals and did not break Jesus’ legs: these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled, not one of his bones will be broken (John 19:33–36), echoing the Passover lamb and this psalm together. So the righteous one on whom the Lord’s eyes rested most of all was the one whose afflictions were greatest, and his deliverance came through death to resurrection. That is the road by which the good days of verse 10 reach his people.

Does this mean that if I live well, life will go well? Generally, yes, and Scripture is not ashamed to say so: honest, peaceable, kind people usually have better lives than liars and brawlers. But it is not a guarantee of comfort in this life, as the very next verses show. Christ lived perfectly and was crucified. The good days promised are finally the days of the age to come, though many are tasted now. So the psalm gives both a practical wisdom and a final hope. Live this way because it is right, because it usually goes better, and because God is watching, and leave the timing of the good days to him.

On a Tuesday. Pick one relationship that is broken or strained, at home, at work, in church, and pursue peace in it this week: an apology, a message, an invitation, a conversation you have been avoiding. And set a guard on your mouth. Before you speak in a tense moment, ask: is this evil, is this deceit, will this pursue peace?

verseByVerse.quote: Now who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good? But even if you should suffer for righteousness' sake, you will be blessed. Have no fear of them, nor be troubled,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good? Harm, kakōsōn, means do evil to, injure. Zealous, zēlōtai, means eager, passionate: the word from which the Jewish revolutionaries called Zealots took their name, and one of Peter’s fellow disciples was known as Simon the Zealot (Luke 6:15). Peter wants a zeal for good as hot as any revolutionary’s. The question expects the answer nobody, and then verse 14 immediately concedes that somebody might. That is not a contradiction; it is a distinction between two kinds of harm. Ordinarily, a life of conspicuous good does disarm hostility, and Peter has already made that his strategy (2:12, 15). And ultimately no one can harm the believer’s soul (Matthew 10:28; Romans 8:31).

Even if you should suffer. Even if, ei kai, with the rare Greek optative, suggests a real but not constant possibility: it may happen. Peter is a realist, and he knows what happened to his Lord. For righteousness’ sake, dia dikaiosynēn, means because of doing right, because of loyalty to Christ. And blessed, makarioi, is the Beatitude word: blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5:10–12). Peter is echoing his Lord almost word for word. So the answer to who can harm you? is that they can hurt you and cannot harm you. The worst they can do lands on a man who is thereby called blessed, which means the injury does not reach the part of him that matters.

Have no fear of them, nor be troubled. The words are from Isaiah 8:12, and the context there is worth knowing. Judah was terrified of an alliance of Syria and Israel forming against it, and of the might of Assyria behind them, and Isaiah was told not to fear what the people feared, but to regard the LORD of hosts as holy and let him be their fear (Isaiah 8:12–13), which is the next verse Peter quotes. Fear of them, ton phobon autōn, can mean the fear they cause or the things they fear, and both fit. Troubled, tarachthēte, means shaken, agitated, stirred up like water. Two commands, and they are different. Do not fear them deals with the object; do not be troubled deals with the inner state, the agitation that persists after the threat has passed. Peter addresses both, and neither is a demand to feel nothing. Isaiah’s word to a frightened nation was not that the danger was imaginary. It was that God was bigger.

What kind of suffering counts as for righteousness’ sake? Suffering that comes because you belong to Christ or because you did what was right: losing a promotion because you would not lie, being mocked for your faith, rejected by family for following Christ, punished for refusing to sin. It does not include suffering that comes from your own foolishness, rudeness or wrongdoing (2:20; 4:15), nor ordinary troubles that come to everyone, though God uses those too. Be careful not to call every criticism persecution. But when the suffering really is for Christ, do not be ashamed. You are in the line of the prophets, and Christ calls you blessed.

For worship. No one can harm those whom God has blessed. Kings may rage and crowds may jeer, but the one who calls his people blessed is the one who holds the keys of death and Hades. He was persecuted for righteousness’ sake as no one ever was, and the kingdom of heaven is his. And he shares it with every one of his persecuted people, so that the prison cell, the empty desk and the family table where they sit alone become places where heaven’s blessing rests.

verseByVerse.quote: but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Honor Christ the Lord as holy. This is the positive replacement for the fear just forbidden, and the logic is displacement: one fear drives out another. It is Isaiah 8:13, the verse after the one just quoted. Peter does the same, with one change he clearly intends. Isaiah’s the LORD of hosts becomes Christ the Lord. In Isaiah the LORD is Yahweh, the covenant God of Israel; Peter applies the verse directly to Christ, without a word of explanation. Christ is the LORD. It is a strong, almost casual, statement of his deity. What does that mean for a frightened believer? That the one he is asked to honour above the magistrate is not a martyred teacher who needs defending but the LORD of hosts himself. Honour as holy, hagiasate, means sanctify, set apart, revere: enthrone Christ in your heart as Lord. The heart that has Christ on its throne has no room left there for the magistrate.

Always being prepared to make a defense. Prepared, hetoimoi, ready. Defence, apologia, is a reasoned answer, the speech for the defence in a courtroom, and our word apologetics comes from it. For these readers that was not always metaphorical. Christians should be able to explain why they believe, whether in a courtroom or a conversation, and always means at any moment, without notice.

A reason for the hope. Asks, aitounti, can mean demands as well as requests. Reason, logos, is an account, an explanation. Hope is the living hope of 1:3. Look at the situation Peter assumes. They are not going out to argue; they are being asked. Somebody has noticed something and enquired. Which means the hope that is in you must have been visible enough to prompt a question, and a Christian whose life raises no questions will rarely be asked. And observe what they are asked to explain. Not the doctrine of the atonement in general, but the hope in you: why you are like this, under these conditions. It is personal testimony grounded in reasons, which is why always being prepared means having thought about it in advance.

Gentleness and respect. Then the manner, and it is half the verse though it is usually the forgotten half. Gentleness, prautēs, is the noun of the word used of the wife in verse 4: strength under control, towards the person asking. Respect is literally fear, phobos, most likely reverence towards God, though it certainly rules out contempt for the questioner. Either way the point stands: an answer given harshly has not obeyed this verse, however correct its content. How we answer matters as much as what we say. Peter is describing a man who honours Christ in his heart, and it comes out as courtesy to the person interrogating him.

What should I actually say if someone asks why I believe? Keep it simple, honest and centred on Christ. Say who Jesus is: God the Son who became man. What he did: lived a perfect life, died in the place of sinners, rose again. Why you trust him: perhaps the evidence of the resurrection, the way Scripture has proved true in your life, the change he has made in you, the forgiveness you have found. And what your hope is: that because of him you are forgiven, and death is not the end. You do not need to answer every objection on the spot. It is fine to say, that is a good question; let me think about it and come back to you, and then do.

What if I am shy or afraid I will say it badly? Then remember that Peter, who once could not say I know him to a servant girl, wrote this verse. God uses ordinary words from ordinary people. Prepare a little: write down in a few sentences why you are a Christian, and read it over until it is your own. Pray for opportunities and for courage. And remember that gentleness and respect, which shy people often have in abundance, are half the command. A quiet, kind, honest answer often does more than a brilliant argument.

verseByVerse.quote: having a good conscience, so that, when you are slandered, those who revile your good behavior in Christ may be put to shame. For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God's will, than for doing evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having a good conscience. Good conscience, syneidēsis agathē, is a conscience that does not accuse, because one has lived rightly: Paul could say, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day (Acts 23:1; 1 Timothy 1:5, 19). Not sinlessness, for no wife, husband or witness obeys perfectly, but integrity: sins confessed, wrongs put right, nothing hidden, all of it resting on the Righteous One who obeyed perfectly in our place (v. 18), whose obedience is counted as ours. The defence of verse 15 requires a life to stand on. A man with something to hide cannot give a straight answer about his hope, because he knows the follow-up question.

When you are slandered. Slandered, katalaleisthe, spoken against, as in 2:12. Again Peter says when. He has assumed the slander throughout the letter, and here he describes precisely how it is defeated.

Put to shame. Revile, epēreazontes, means insult, mistreat, abuse. Good behaviour in Christ, agathēn en Christō anastrophēn, is good conduct flowing from union with Christ. Put to shame, kataischynthōsin, means be embarrassed, exposed as wrong. The mechanism is exposure. The accusation is made publicly; the life is then observed publicly; and the gap between them shames the accuser. Peter is not promising the slander will stop, and he is not recommending a rebuttal. He is saying that a sufficiently clean life eventually embarrasses the people describing it falsely. And there is a sharp phrase inside it: they revile your good behaviour in Christ. What is actually being attacked is not the Christians but Christ in them, which is why the conduct matters so much and why the vindication is finally his.

Better to suffer for doing good. The most carefully worded sentence in the paragraph, and two things in it matter. First, the comparison assumes suffering either way and simply asks which kind. That is bleak and it is honest: Peter never suggests the alternative to suffering for righteousness is no suffering at all. If we must suffer, let it be for doing good, not for wrongdoing (2:20; 4:15). Second, and most important: if that should be God’s will, ei theloi to thelēma tou theou. Suffering comes only within God’s will (4:19); he is sovereign over it. Peter will not let unjust suffering be described as an accident, an oversight, or the devil’s victory. It falls inside the will of God, which is either intolerable or the only thing that makes it bearable, and this letter has been arguing for the second since chapter 1.

My conscience still troubles me about past sins. Can I have a good conscience? Yes, through the blood of Christ, which purifies our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14). A good conscience is not one that has never sinned, but one that has been cleansed and is kept clean by confession and repentance. If there is something you can still put right, a debt, an apology, a lie to correct, do it. Then rest on Christ’s forgiveness. If your conscience goes on accusing you over sins already confessed and forgiven, it is no longer telling the truth; answer it with the gospel, and if it persists, talk to a pastor.

On a Tuesday. Is there anything in your life you would not want a hostile neighbour to find out? Christ’s blood is enough to cleanse it (Hebrews 9:14), so bring it into the light this week: confess it and put it right. Then, when the accusation comes, you will have nothing to fear from the follow-up question.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — Christ's Suffering and Cosmic Victory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter grounds the call to suffer well in Christ’s own path, from the cross to the throne. The middle of the passage (the spirits in prison, Noah, baptism) is among the hardest in the New Testament, but its point is plain: Christ has triumphed over every power, and God brings his few safely through.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ’s Victory

Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God. Verses 19–20 are disputed, but no reading offers a second chance after death.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Noah's household of eight was a small minority brought safely through.

Now: Every power believers fear has already been made subject to the risen Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Christ also suffered once for sins. The for connects it to verse 17: if unjust suffering can be God’s will, here is the supreme case of it. And also: Christ is the supreme example of suffering for doing good. But at once Peter moves beyond example. Once, hapax, means once for all, never to be repeated. It is the word Hebrews builds its argument on (Hebrews 9:26–28), and it rules out any notion of a sacrifice that must be topped up, repeated or re-presented. His suffering was unique and complete. For sins, peri hamartiōn, is the phrase used in the Greek Old Testament for the sin offering. His death was a sacrifice for sin.

The righteous for the unrighteous. Four words in English, and they are as compact a statement of substitution as the New Testament contains. Righteous, dikaios: Christ, the sinless one, the Holy and Righteous One whom Peter had preached to the crowds in the temple (Acts 3:14). For, hyper, on behalf of, in place of. Unrighteous, adikōn: us, sinners. Singular and plural: one righteous man in the place of many unrighteous ones. And the exchange is not a transaction between equals: it is the innocent standing where the guilty were (2 Corinthians 5:21; Romans 5:6–8). This is penal substitution, the righteous one bearing the penalty due to the guilty, in a single phrase. Barabbas, released while Jesus was led away, is its picture.

That he might bring us to God. Bring, prosagagē, means lead to, usher into the presence of, as a courtier introduces someone to the king; in the Greek Old Testament it is used of bringing a sacrifice to the altar and of presenting priests for consecration. The purpose of the cross is stated as access (Ephesians 2:18; 3:12). Not primarily to make us safe or happy but to bring us into a presence we had no business entering, and that names what salvation is finally for. The end is not an improved life or even an escaped hell. It is God himself, and everything else is arrangements for getting there.

Put to death, made alive. Put to death in the flesh, thanatōtheis sarki: he truly died, physically, in his human body. Made alive in the spirit, zōopoiētheis pneumati: either in the Spirit, by the Holy Spirit who raised him (Romans 8:11), or in the spiritual realm, the realm of the Spirit and of his resurrection life. The two datives are parallel and describe two spheres: killed as far as earthly, mortal human life goes; made alive in the realm of the Spirit, the new creation. It refers to his resurrection, in which he was raised in a glorified body empowered by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 15:45; Romans 1:4; 1 Timothy 3:16). And it sets up the notoriously difficult verse that follows.

What does made alive in the spirit mean? Some take it as Christ’s human spirit living on after death; others as the Holy Spirit by whom he was raised (Romans 8:11). The more likely reading is that Peter contrasts two spheres: put to death in the realm of the flesh, raised to life in the realm of the Spirit, the new resurrection life.

What it does not mean. Made alive in the spirit does not mean Jesus’ body stayed dead and only his spirit lived on. He rose bodily (Luke 24:39). Nor does it mean his human spirit died; at death, his spirit went to the Father (Luke 23:46).

If Christ suffered once for all, why do Christians still suffer? Because his suffering for sins and our suffering for righteousness are different things. He suffered to pay for sin, and that is finished; nothing we suffer adds to it or pays for anything. Our sufferings are not punishment for sin, which has been fully borne, but the path of a disciple following his Master to glory (2:21; 4:13). Christ’s once-for-all suffering means your suffering can never be God’s condemnation. It can only be his discipline, his refining, and the fellowship of the cross. That changes how you bear it. You suffer as one already brought to God.

How do I come to God through Christ? By trusting him. Peter says Christ died to bring us to God, and the way in is not by improving yourself first, or by any ceremony, but by faith: admitting you are among the unrighteous, believing that the Righteous One died in your place and rose again, and coming to God on that basis alone. If you have never done that, you can do it now, in your own words, in prayer. And if you are a believer who feels far from God, the same verse applies. The door Christ opened is still open. Come in again.

verseByVerse.quote: in which he went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison, because they formerly did not obey, when God's patience waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being prepared, in which a few, that is, eight persons, were brought safely through water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The spirits in prison. The plain point first: whatever the details mean, Christ has triumphed over every evil power, and God brings his few safely through judgement. The details are among the most disputed in the New Testament, and honesty about that serves better than confidence. Godly readers have differed for centuries, and Luther confessed that he did not know for certain what Peter meant. The main views: (1) between his death and resurrection, Christ went to the realm of the dead and preached the gospel to the souls of those who died in Noah’s flood, giving them a second chance; (2) between his death and resurrection, Christ descended to the place of the dead and announced his victory to the dead, without offering a second chance; (3) after his resurrection, in his ascension, Christ proclaimed his victory to fallen angels (spirits) imprisoned for their sin in Noah’s day (2 Peter 2:4–5; Jude 6; Genesis 6:1–4); (4) Christ, by the Spirit, preached through Noah to the people of Noah’s day, who rejected the message and are now spirits in prison (in hell).

The words themselves. In which, en hō: in the Spirit, or in the spiritual realm, the sphere just named. Proclaimed, ekēryxen, means heralded, announced: it is the herald’s word, not necessarily the gospel, for a herald may announce victory or judgement. Peter does not use the word for preaching good news here. Spirits, pneumasin: in the New Testament, used alone, this word usually means angelic beings, not human souls (Hebrews 1:14; Matthew 8:16). In prison, en phylakē, means under guard. And went, poreutheis, is the same participle as in verse 22, he has gone into heaven, which suggests that the going in both verses may be one journey: the risen Christ on his way to the Father’s right hand.

God’s patience waited. Did not obey, apeithēsasin, disobeyed. God’s patience waited, apexedecheto hē tou theou makrothymia: God waited, perhaps 120 years (Genesis 6:3), while Noah built and preached, a herald of righteousness (2 Peter 2:5). Jewish writings of Peter’s day, especially the book of 1 Enoch, which Jude quotes (Jude 14–15), told at length of the angels who sinned before the flood and were bound in darkness until the judgement, and Peter’s readers would very likely have heard of them. Whatever else the verse means, it shows God’s patience: he waited a long time before the waters came.

Eight persons. Noah, his wife, his three sons and their wives (Genesis 7:13). Brought safely through, diesōthēsan, were saved through. The water that destroyed the world carried the ark to safety: the same water was judgement to some and rescue to others. And the pastoral point survives every reading, which is presumably why Peter included it. Noah’s family was a tiny minority in a world entirely against him, and God’s patience waited while he built. That is the situation of the people receiving this letter, a small, persecuted minority in Pontus and Bithynia, and the eight were not lost.

Where Christians differ: did Christ offer the dead a second chance? This commentary’s view: The view that Christ offered salvation to the dead contradicts Scripture’s clear teaching that destiny is fixed at death (Luke 16:26; Hebrews 9:27), and it would be strange to offer it only to Noah’s generation. The two strongest views are the third (Christ, in his resurrection and ascension, proclaimed his triumph over the fallen angels imprisoned since Noah’s day, as 2 Peter 2:4–5 and Jude 6 describe) and the fourth (Christ by his Spirit preached through Noah to those who are now in prison). The third fits the word spirits, the link with verse 22 (angels subjected to him), and the context of Christ’s victory. It takes the sons of God of Genesis 6:1–4 as angels who sinned, as many Jewish and early Christian readers did, a link the order of 2 Peter 2:4–6 and Jude 6–7 supports; Calvin and many Reformed writers read them as the godly line of Seth. The angel reading is the more likely one, held without dogmatism. Either way, the point is clear: Christ suffered and was vindicated; he triumphed over every evil power; and his people, though few and persecuted like Noah’s family, will be saved. There is no second chance after death, and no purgatory.

Why the third view is preferred. It also fits Paul’s picture: he disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him (Colossians 2:15). The fourth view has real strength in the immediate mention of Noah’s preaching, and many good Reformed interpreters have held it.

Does this teach that Christ descended into hell, as the Apostles’ Creed says? The creed’s phrase has been read in several ways. Calvin and the Heidelberg Catechism (Q. 44) understand it of the hellish anguish Christ suffered in his soul on the cross; the Westminster Larger Catechism (Q. 50) of his continuing in the state of the dead, under the power of death, until the third day. This verse is often linked to it, but Peter speaks of Christ proclaiming in which, in the Spirit, to the spirits in prison, and the more likely reading, as the verdict above holds, is the risen Christ announcing his victory to rebellious spirits; others take it of Christ preaching through Noah to the people of Noah’s day, who are now in prison. Either way, it is not a second chance for the dead, and it is not a further suffering.

What about people who never heard the gospel? This verse does not teach that they will get a chance after death, and Scripture gives no such hope (Hebrews 9:27). Salvation is through conscious faith in Christ (Acts 4:12; Romans 10:13–17), which is why the church is sent to the ends of the earth with urgency. We can trust that the Judge of all the earth will do right (Genesis 18:25), that no one will be condemned for anything but their own sin against the light they had (Romans 1:20; 2:12), and that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3; the Westminster Confession 10.3). Parents who have lost a little one may rest on the kindness of the Lord who took children in his arms (Mark 10:16), and many Reformed pastors have gone further and hoped, with good reason, that all who die in infancy are among his own. But the right response to the question is not speculation; it is mission. Peter’s point is that God waited patiently in Noah’s day, and he is waiting patiently now, while the gospel goes out (2 Peter 3:9).

On a Tuesday. If you feel outnumbered as a Christian, at work, at school, in your family, remember Noah’s eight, and remember that numbers did not decide who was safe. The ark did. Keep building, keep obeying, keep speaking, and trust the God who waits patiently and then acts. And give thanks that the powers behind the hostility you face have already heard their sentence announced by the risen Christ.

For worship. While the whole world mocked, God shut eight people safely into the ark, and the waters that drowned the world lifted them up. Now the risen Christ has gone up through every realm of darkness, a herald of his own victory, and the rebel spirits in their prison have heard that they are defeated. There is no power left that can claim his people. The God who waited in Noah’s day is waiting still, with long patience, and when the door is shut, every one of his own will be inside, carried through the judgement by the one who bore it for them.
verseByVerse.note: One of the hardest passages in the New Testament. Main views: Christ preached through Noah to the people of his day; or after his death he proclaimed victory to fallen angels imprisoned for the sins of Noah’s time.

verseByVerse.quote: Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you, not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Baptism, which corresponds to this. This needs careful reading, not alarm or overstatement. Corresponds, antitypon, means antitype, counterpart, the fulfilment of a pattern: the thing the earlier pattern pointed to. The flood was a type or picture; baptism is its counterpart. The flood pattern is: judgement falls, water is the instrument, and a few are brought safely through it in the ark into a new world. As Noah’s family passed through the waters of judgement in the ark and were saved, so believers pass through the waters of baptism in Christ. The water of baptism pictures the judgement that fell on Christ, the ark of his people, and our coming through it with him into new creation.

Now saves you. Saves, sōzei. A surprising statement, and Peter immediately qualifies it, which settles the matter. He raises the strongest way of putting it, and in the same breath rules out the mechanical reading.

Not a removal of dirt. The water itself does not save. The water does nothing; a Jew who washed for ritual purity, or a pagan bathed in an initiation rite, would gain nothing from it before God, and neither would a baptised man without faith.

An appeal to God. Appeal, eperōtēma, can mean a request, a pledge, or the answer to a question. Either it is the cry of a man asking God to give him a clear conscience, or it is the pledge of a good conscience given to God, the response made at baptism to the question, do you believe? The word was later used in contracts for the formal question and answer that sealed an agreement. Either way it locates the saving power in what is happening between the person and God, not in the liquid. Baptism saves as the outward expression of inward faith, the believer’s commitment to God and request for cleansing, based on Christ’s work.

Through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. And there is the final safeguard. The saving power is not in the water but in Christ’s resurrection (1:3). Baptism saves the way a wedding ring marries you: it is the sign and pledge of a union whose power lies entirely elsewhere. What saves is the risen Christ; baptism is how a person is joined to him publicly and says so. It unites us symbolically with Christ in his death and resurrection: we were buried therefore with him by baptism into death (Romans 6:3–4; Colossians 2:12), and faith receives the reality.

At the right hand of God. His ascension and enthronement (Acts 1:9–11; Hebrews 1:3). Peter had stood on the Mount of Olives and watched him go, and had preached at Pentecost that God had exalted him at his right hand (Acts 2:33). The right hand is the place of authority, honour and rule. The man who was put to death in the flesh is now seated on the throne of the universe.

Angels, authorities, and powers. Subjected, hypotagentōn, placed under: the same family as the be subject that has run through the letter (2:13, 18; 3:1). The Christian who submits to the emperor for the Lord’s sake serves a Lord to whom every power in heaven and earth has already been made subject. All spiritual powers, good and evil, are under Christ’s authority, far above all rule and authority and power and dominion (Ephesians 1:20–22; Colossians 2:15). This is the letter’s whole answer to intimidation. Every power these readers were afraid of, the magistrate, the mob, the emperor, and whatever stood behind them, is named and placed. Subjected, past tense, already done. The man they follow was rejected by men (2:4), suffered unjustly (2:23), and is now seated with the authorities under his feet; and that is the sequence Peter has been asking them to trust for their own lives since the first verse.

Where Christians differ: does baptism itself save? Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and some others hold that baptism conveys regeneration and forgiveness, and they are taking Scripture’s strong words about baptism seriously. This commentary’s view: Peter explicitly denies that the water itself saves (not as a removal of dirt from the body). Baptism saves as the appeal or pledge of a good conscience, that is, as the expression of faith, through Christ’s resurrection. The sign is so closely tied to the reality it signifies that Scripture can speak of the sign as doing what the reality does, as when the Lord’s Supper is called the body of Christ. Salvation comes through faith in the risen Christ; baptism is the outward sign of that faith, rightly given to those who profess it.

Does Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you mean that baptism gives new birth? Roman Catholic, Lutheran and some other Christians read it so. But Peter explains immediately: not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. What saves is not the water but what baptism expresses, a heart turning to God and trusting the risen Christ. That is why baptism belongs to those who can make that appeal. This is the conviction of the 1689 London Baptist Confession (29.2), that those who actually profess repentance towards God and faith in Christ are the proper subjects of baptism. Our paedobaptist brothers in the Reformed churches, who baptise the children of believers as a sign of the covenant, agree with us that the water does not regenerate; we differ in love on who should receive the sign, and gladly share the same Saviour.

I am a believer but have never been baptised. Should I be? Yes. Baptism is Christ’s command to every disciple (Matthew 28:19; Acts 2:38), and it is the way he appointed for you to confess him publicly and be joined visibly to his people. You are not saved by it, but you are called to it, and holding back disobeys the Lord you love. If fear, embarrassment or uncertainty is stopping you, talk to your pastor. And remember the thief on the cross: those who truly believe but die before they can be baptised are not lost. The command is for those who have the opportunity, and you do.

Why is Christ’s reign over the powers good news for me today? Because whatever is pressing on you, a hostile boss, a government that opposes Christians, an addiction, fear of the dark spiritual forces Scripture speaks of, is already under his feet. Nothing has authority over you that he does not allow, and nothing can separate you from his love (Romans 8:38–39). You do not have to defeat the powers; he already has. Your task is to stand firm in him, resist the devil (5:9), and trust that the one at God’s right hand is ruling all things for the good of his church (Ephesians 1:22).

On a Tuesday. Remember your baptism today, not as a ceremony in the past but as a pledge you made to God and he sealed: I belong to the risen Christ. When temptation comes, say it. When fear comes, say it. And when you are tempted to think the powers of this world are in charge, look up. There is a man on the throne of heaven, and every authority is under him.
