4.title: Stewards of Grace: The Meaning of Suffering
4.overview: Chapter 4 returns to suffering in the light of the end: “The end of all things is at hand” (v. 7). The first half (vv. 1–11) shows how suffering settles a believer’s break with the old life, and how a church facing the end should live: clear-headed for prayer, loving earnestly, hospitable, and using every gift for others. The second half (vv. 12–19) speaks directly to the fiery trial, and ends with entrusting the soul to a faithful Creator.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Stewards of God's Varied Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter shows how Christ’s suffering settles a believer’s break with the old life, and why old friends find that break so strange. Then, with the end near, he describes a church that prays, loves, welcomes and serves, so that God is glorified through Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
Stewards of God's Varied Grace

Suffering for Christ settles a believer's break with sin. Because the end is near, stay clear-headed for prayer, love earnestly, and use each gift to serve others.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Neighbours were baffled when converts no longer joined them, and spoke against them.

Now: Love covers a multitude of sins: it does not pass offences around.

verseByVerse.quote: Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, for whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin, so as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Peter 4 prepares believers to live for God in a world that mocks them. Christ suffered in the flesh, so they arm themselves with the same mind, finished with living for desire (vv. 1–2). Old friends are surprised and slander them, but will give account to the Judge of the living and the dead; believers who have died live with God (vv. 3–6). The end is near: pray with clear minds, love deeply, since love covers many sins, welcome one another without grumbling, and use every gift as stewards of God’s grace, so that God is glorified through Christ (vv. 7–11). The fiery trial is no surprise: they share Christ’s sufferings, and the Spirit of glory rests on them (vv. 12–14). Never suffer as wrongdoers; suffering as a Christian is no shame (vv. 15–16). Judgement begins with God’s household, so those who suffer entrust themselves to a faithful Creator and keep doing good (vv. 17–19).

Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh. Therefore picks up 3:18: Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous. In the flesh, sarki: in his body, physically, to death. Peter has just shown Christ enthroned above all powers (3:22). Now he turns back to the road that led there, and tells his readers that it is their road too.

Arm yourselves with the same way of thinking. Arm yourselves, hoplisasthe, is a soldier’s word: put on armour, take up your weapons, the word behind the Greek hoplite, the heavy infantryman. And what Peter hands them is not a shield but a thought. Way of thinking, ennoia, is mindset, attitude, settled resolve. The thought is the settled conviction that suffering is the road Christ took. His attitude was willingness to suffer rather than sin, and to do God’s will at any cost. A Christian ambushed by suffering he did not expect is far more likely to collapse than one who decided in advance what it means. Peter is telling them to make the decision before the trial rather than during it. Soldiers do not put their armour on after the arrows start flying. And the armour is not our resolve alone: the Spirit who raised Christ supplies the strength (Romans 8:11–13).

Ceased from sin. Then the difficult clause. Read flatly it seems to say that suffering makes a person sinless, which is plainly untrue and contradicts the commands that follow. Two readings carry weight. It may refer to Christ himself: he suffered and is now done with sin, having dealt with it once for all (3:18). Or, more likely given the whoever, it describes what suffering does to a believer’s relationship with sin. The person who has made a decisive break with sin, embracing suffering for Christ rather than compromise, has thereby shown that sin no longer rules him (Romans 6:7). He has already chosen, under pressure, and the choosing settles something. It may also allude to union with Christ’s death: having died with him, we are finished with sin as a master.

For the will of God. Verse 2 supports the second reading by stating the result. The rest of the time is the remainder of earthly life. Human passions, anthrōpōn epithymiais, are the desires of people, what everyone around you wants. The great reorientation: from living for desires to living for God. The break is about direction, not perfection: we never live for God’s will flawlessly, but Christ did, all the way to the cross, and his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19). And anyone who has suffered for a conviction knows the effect. Once you have lost something real for Christ, the appeal of what you gave up is permanently reduced: you have already found out what it was worth. That is not sinlessness. It is a man who has stopped negotiating.

What does arming myself look like in practice? It means settling now, in a calm hour, what you will do when obedience becomes costly, so that you are not deciding in the heat of the moment. Decide in advance that you will not lie for your employer, that you will not join the mockery of the colleague, that you will tell your family you are a Christian, that you would rather lose the deal than cut the corner. Think through what it might cost, and pray it through. Read the accounts of Christ’s passion until his mindset becomes familiar. Then, when the moment comes, you will find that the armour is already on.

verseByVerse.quote: For the time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do, living in sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry. With respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them in the same flood of debauchery, and they malign you;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The time that is past suffices. Suffices, arketos: is enough. The understatement is almost dry: you have given that quite enough of your life already. Peter does not argue them out of their old habits; he simply says the account is closed. Gentiles here means pagans, unbelievers (2:12), and Peter’s readers were mostly former pagans. What the Gentiles want to do is the will of the culture, set against the will of God of verse 2.

Six words. Sensuality, aselgeiai: unrestrained immorality, shameless excess. Passions, epithymiai: lusts. Drunkenness, oinophlygiai: literally overflowing with wine. Orgies, kōmoi: carousing, wild revelry, the drunken processions that wound through the streets at night, often linked to the cult of Dionysus. Drinking parties, potoi: drinking bouts. Lawless idolatry, athemitoi eidōlolatriai: abominable, forbidden idolatry. Much of it was religious: the temple feasts of a Greek city and the banquets of the trade guilds, held in temple dining rooms in honour of the guild’s patron god, ran on exactly this, and the last item names what held the rest together. Nearly the whole list is social, things done in company, which is precisely why leaving it cost these people their friends, and often their livelihoods.

They are surprised. Surprised, xenizontai, means to be taken aback, to think something strange, thrown by something unaccountable. The word is related to xenos, stranger: the Christians have become strangers in their own town. Their neighbours are genuinely puzzled: not offended on principle but bewildered that anyone would opt out, and Christians came to be seen as antisocial, odd, and disloyal to civic religion.

In the same flood of debauchery. Join, syntrechontōn, means run together with, rush along with. Flood, anachysis, is a vivid word: an outpouring, a torrent, something running out of its channel like a drain overflowing. Debauchery, asōtia, is wild living, dissipation, the word Luke uses (in its adverb form) of the prodigal son, who squandered his property in reckless living (Luke 15:13). And the picture explains the reaction. When everyone is being carried along by a current, the person standing still is not merely different; he is an implied criticism of everyone moving past him.

And they malign you. Malign, blasphēmountes: slander, abuse, speak evil of. They mocked and slandered the Christians, perhaps as killjoys, haters of humanity, or atheists; the Roman historian Tacitus could describe the Christians as hated for their abominations and convicted of hatred of the human race. That is the mechanism of the slander this whole letter addresses. It does not begin in theological objection. It begins in social withdrawal: you stopped coming, and the people you stopped coming to have drawn their own conclusions about why.

Ransomed from the futile ways. The break with that life was not a matter of willpower. Peter told these readers that they were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from their forefathers with the precious blood of Christ (1:18–19). The current they once ran with was a slavery, and someone paid to get them out. And when the neighbours malign them for it, they walk where their Lord walked. He was called a glutton and a drunkard by people who could not tell eating with sinners from sinning with them (Matthew 11:19). He went to the table and never into the flood. The Christian maligned for standing still is being treated as his Master was.

Does this mean Christians should avoid social occasions with unbelievers altogether? No. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners (Luke 7:34), and Paul says we cannot leave the world (1 Corinthians 5:9–10). Peter warns against joining in the excesses: drunkenness, orgies, idolatry. A Christian may be at the party; he should not be part of what the party becomes.

How do I handle friends who mock me for not joining in? With good humour, honesty and kindness. You do not need to preach at them or explain yourself at length; a simple, cheerful I would rather not is often enough. Keep up the friendship in other ways: invite them for a meal, help them move house, be there when life goes wrong for them. They are often more watchful than they seem, and many who mock now will one day come to the one friend who did not join in. Do not be bitter if some drift away. And find Christian friends too, so that you are not standing in the current alone.

On a Tuesday. Look honestly at your own life: is there a part of the old flood you have quietly gone back to, perhaps in what you watch, or how much you drink, or how you talk? You were ransomed out of it with Christ’s blood, and his Spirit is in you to keep you out of it. The time that is past suffices. Do not give it any more.

verseByVerse.quote: but they will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. For this is why the gospel was preached even to those who are dead, that though judged in the flesh the way people are, they might live in the spirit the way God does.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will give account. Give account, apodōsousin logon, means render an account, as a steward does to his master. The answer to being maligned is not vindication now but a court later: the same move as 2:23, where Christ entrusted himself to the one who judges justly. The slanderers will answer to God. Ready, hetoimōs, is the sharp word: he is standing by, and the delay is patience rather than absence. Judge the living and the dead may refer to Christ or to God the Father, and Scripture says both; Peter himself had told Cornelius that Christ is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead (Acts 10:42; 2 Timothy 4:1). All people, whether alive at his return or already dead, will be judged.

Is a God who judges not at odds with a God of love? Only if love is indifferent to evil. A God who never judged would be telling every slandered Christian in Bithynia, every abused child and every murdered martyr that what was done to them did not matter. Love that is not angry at what destroys the beloved is not love at all. The Bible’s God is slow to anger and ready to judge, and those two belong together: his patience gives time to repent (2 Peter 3:9), and his judgement means no wrong is finally swept aside. And the Judge of the living and the dead is the one who was judged for sinners at the cross, so that all who come to him find the verdict already borne (Romans 8:1).

Even to those who are dead. Another genuinely disputed sentence. Those who are dead, nekrois: most likely Christians who have since died, people who heard the gospel while alive and are now dead, perhaps through martyrdom, perhaps through ordinary death. That was a live pastoral problem: believers had been dying, sometimes under persecution, and the obvious taunt from neighbours was that their faith had done them no good at all. Some in the churches may have wondered the same, as the Thessalonians had (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). Peter answers that the gospel was preached to them in life for this very purpose.

Judged in the flesh. Judged in the flesh, krithōsi sarki: they suffered physical death, the common human judgement for sin (Romans 5:12), or they were condemned by human courts, or both. The way people are, kata anthrōpous: according to human standards, in human eyes. The verdict of death was passed on them as it is on everyone. It was not the last word.

Live in the spirit. Live in the spirit, zōsi pneumati: they are alive in God’s presence, in the spiritual realm, awaiting the resurrection, the spirits of the righteous made perfect (Hebrews 12:23; Revelation 6:9–11). The way God does, kata theon: according to God, in God’s estimation. Human verdict: condemned and dead. God’s verdict: alive.

The shape of Christ’s own death. The shape of verse 6 is the shape of Christ’s own death and vindication, which Peter described a few sentences earlier in almost the same words (3:18). Christ, too, was judged in the flesh the way people are: condemned by a human court and executed as a criminal. And God reversed the verdict by raising him. The believers whom Bithynia buried are following their Lord down the same road and up out of it. That is why the Judge of the living and the dead is no terror to them: he has stood under the world’s sentence himself, and come out alive on the far side.

Where Christians differ: does this teach a second chance after death? Some read this verse, alongside 3:19, as teaching that the gospel is preached to the dead in the afterlife, giving them an opportunity to believe. This commentary’s view: The verb is past tense (was preached), and the most natural reading is that the gospel was preached to people while they were alive, who are now dead. Scripture consistently teaches that death fixes one’s destiny (Luke 16:26; Hebrews 9:27). There is no second chance after death. The verse comforts believers: those who died in Christ are not lost but live with God.

Does this offer a second chance after death? Some early writers read it as preaching to the dead in Hades; others link it to 3:19. The more likely reading is that the gospel was preached to believers while they were alive, who have since died; though they suffered judgement in the flesh, they live with God. Scripture offers no second chance after death (Hebrews 9:27). The alternative reading empties the urgency of the New Testament’s own preaching, and it is not needed, because the natural reading is both simpler and more comforting.

Where are Christians who have died, and what are they doing? With Christ, consciously, in joy. Paul says that to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). They are not asleep in the sense of unconscious, nor waiting in purgatory to be purified; Christ’s blood has already done that. They rest from their labours (Revelation 14:13), worship, and wait with longing for the resurrection of the body at Christ’s return, when they will come with him and we will be reunited (1 Thessalonians 4:14–17). Grieve for them, but not as those who have no hope.

On a Tuesday. Think of a believer you have known who has died. Thank God for them by name, and remind yourself, in Peter’s words, where they are: alive with God.

verseByVerse.quote: The end of all things is at hand; therefore be self-controlled and sober-minded for the sake of your prayers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The end of all things is at hand. The word for end is telos: not merely the stopping but the goal, the completion, the point everything has been heading for. Peter is not announcing that things will run out; he is saying they will arrive. All things means the present age, history itself. At hand, ēngiken, has drawn near, as in James 5:8. The death and resurrection of Christ have brought the end near. The next great event in God’s plan is Christ’s return, which is always near: no date is given, and every generation must live ready.

Why near? And at hand has drawn a great deal of comment, since two thousand years have passed. The New Testament’s consistent posture is not a calculated date but a nearness that makes everything urgent. The last days began at Pentecost (Acts 2:17), and the gathering in of God’s people goes on until the last is in. Scripture does name things that will come first, such as the final rebellion and the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3), but they are no timetable to calculate, for that mystery of lawlessness is already at work (2 Thessalonians 2:7). Peter himself writes that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day (2 Peter 3:8), so near, for him, was never a date on a calendar. Near describes the nature of the whole age: we live on the edge of eternity, and the door could open in any generation, ours included.

Therefore be self-controlled. What he draws from it is startling. Given that the end is near, you might expect a call to dramatic action: evangelise harder, wind up your affairs, gather on a hillside. Peter says: be self-controlled and sober-minded, and pray. Self-controlled, sōphronēsate, means be sensible, of sound mind: the word used of the man from whom Jesus drove the demons, found sitting, clothed and in his right mind (Mark 5:15). Not panicked or carried away by end-time speculation, but clear-headed.

And sober-minded. Sober-minded, nēpsate, is from 1:13 and will come again in 5:8: clear-headed, alert, unintoxicated, seeing things as they are. It is the opposite of the drunkenness of verse 3. Peter’s answer to eschatological urgency is a steady head.

For the sake of your prayers. Literally for prayers. The clear head is not for its own sake. It is so that they can pray, because a mind that is agitated, frightened or intoxicated cannot. Jesus told his disciples to watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation (Mark 14:38), and Peter slept instead, and was asked, could you not watch with me one hour? (Matthew 26:40). Within hours he was denying him. He has learned what a sleeping mind costs, and he had seen the alternative: that night only one mind in the garden was clear, the mind of Jesus, who prayed his way to the end of his own road and then rose and said, the hour has come; rise, let us be going (Mark 14:41–42). Prayer often fails not through unbelief but through mental clutter, and Peter clears the head so that prayer becomes possible again.

Should I try to work out when the end will come? No. Jesus said that concerning that day and hour no one knows (Matthew 24:36), and every generation that has tried to set dates has been embarrassed. Scripture does not teach a secret rapture (the idea that believers will be taken away unseen before a final tribulation); it teaches one visible return of Christ, in glory, to raise the dead, judge the world and make all things new (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). Many dear Christians do expect such a rapture, and they share our longing for his coming; this commentary reads being caught up to meet the Lord as part of his one public return, because Paul describes it with a shout, a trumpet and the dead rising. The right response is not speculation but readiness: a clear mind, a praying heart, a loving life. Live every day as if he might come today, and plan as if he might not come for a hundred years.

How do I clear my head to pray? Begin by noticing what is clogging it: worry, noise, screens, resentment, too much to do. Pray at a time and place where those can be shut out, even for ten minutes: before the phone is switched on, on a walk, in the car with the radio off. Write down the worries that crowd in, then hand each to God. Pray Scripture, which steadies the mind, especially the Psalms. And keep short accounts with God and with others, because unconfessed sin is the loudest distraction of all. A sober mind is not a blank mind; it is a mind turned towards God.

verseByVerse.quote: Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins. Show hospitality to one another without grumbling.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Above all. Above all, pro pantōn, before everything. And earnestly, ektenē, is the word from 1:22: fervent, constant, love that does not slacken. Under persecution, the church must hold together in strong love. A besieged city whose citizens are fighting one another will not last long.

Love covers. The phrase comes from Proverbs 10:12: hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offenses; James uses it too (James 5:20). And covers, kalyptei, hides, overlooks, must be read rightly. This is not concealment of wrongdoing, and it is not the covering that atones; only Christ’s blood does that. It means love does not spread things. It refuses to publish, to exaggerate, to relitigate, to keep the account open (1 Corinthians 13:5, 7). It forgives and overlooks offences. A congregation of perhaps a dozen households under persecution, meeting weekly in someone’s front room, will generate friction constantly; and the difference between a church that survives that and one that tears itself apart is whether small offences get covered or circulated.

Whose sin is covered. Peter knows where this love is learned. Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered, sang David (Psalm 32:1), and the Christian knows what his own covering cost: Christ himself bore our sins in his body on the tree (2:24). A man who has had a multitude of sins covered by that blood is the last man entitled to keep a ledger on his brother. The love that covers is the cross reproduced on a small scale: the forgiven passing on a little of what they have received in full.

Without grumbling. Hospitality, philoxenoi, means love of strangers. And hospitality was not optional in that world. There were no church buildings: the congregation met in a home, and somebody’s floor took the wear. Travelling believers and missionaries needed lodging, since inns were expensive and often had a poor reputation. It was a costly practical burden borne by whoever had the largest room (Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2). Which is exactly why without grumbling, aneu gongysmou, is attached. Peter knows that the household hosting the church is the household most likely to resent it, and that the resentment will come out as muttering rather than refusal. The command is not to open your door; they were already doing that. It is to stop complaining about the cost of it.

Does love covers a multitude of sins mean we should keep quiet about serious sin, abuse or crime? No. Love overlooks many small offences and forgives readily. But serious or unrepentant sin is to be confronted (Matthew 18:15–17; Galatians 6:1), and abuse and crime must be reported to the proper authorities (Romans 13:4). Covering sin in love never means hiding harm from those who need protecting.

How do I know whether to overlook something or raise it? Ask a few questions. Is it a small irritation, a thoughtless word, a matter of personality or preference? Then cover it: forgive it, and do not mention it to others. Is it a pattern that is harming the person or others, a serious sin, or something that is damaging your relationship so that you cannot let it go? Then go to the person privately and gently (Matthew 18:15). Is anyone in danger, or has a crime been committed? Then it must be reported, at once. Love overlooks much but never covers what endangers the vulnerable. When in doubt, ask a wise elder.

What if hospitality is genuinely hard for me? Then start small and start honestly. Hospitality is not about a beautiful house or elaborate food; it is about opening your life to others. A cup of tea, soup and bread, an invitation to Sunday lunch with whatever you were already eating. If your home is not suitable, take someone out for coffee, or help someone else host. If you are exhausted, or ill, or caring for someone, God knows your limits; do what you can, gladly. And notice that Peter forbids the grumbling, not the tiredness. Ask God for a cheerful heart, and remember that some have entertained angels unawares (Hebrews 13:2).

For worship. The Son of God came into his own world as a stranger. Foxes had holes and birds had nests, and he had nowhere of his own to lay his head; he lodged in borrowed rooms and ate at other men’s tables. And the homeless Guest is the great Host. He has made us welcome in his Father’s house, strangers and enemies as we were, gone ahead to prepare a place for us, and set a table where the cost of the meal was his own blood, and he has never once grumbled at it. Every opened door in his church is a small sign of the hospitality of God, who is preparing a feast for his people that will never end.

verseByVerse.quote: As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God's varied grace: whoever speaks, as one who speaks oracles of God; whoever serves, as one who serves by the strength that God supplies—in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As each has received a gift. Each, hekastos: the word carries the weight. Peter assumes that every member of these scattered congregations has been given something, and there is no category of Christian who has not. Gift, charisma, is a grace-gift, as in Romans 12:6 and 1 Corinthians 12:4: given by God’s grace, not earned, and not chosen.

Use it to serve one another. Serve, diakonountes, minister, the word from which deacon comes. The gift is not for the possessor. It arrives already assigned, and the direction is towards other people, which settles the question of what gifts are for before anyone can make them a measure of standing.

Stewards of varied grace. A steward, oikonomos, managed a household that belonged to someone else, often a slave entrusted with the master’s property (Titus 1:7), and he would be asked about it. We do not own our gifts; we manage them for God, and it is required of stewards that they be found faithful (1 Corinthians 4:2). And varied, poikilēs, is a lovely word: literally many-coloured, used of an embroidered cloth. It is the same word as the various trials of 1:6. God’s grace is as many-coloured as our trials, and for every shade of trouble there is a matching shade of grace. The congregation is a fabric of different colours, and a single-coloured church has lost something God intended to be seen.

Oracles of God. Peter divides all gifts into two: whoever speaks and whoever serves. Word and deed, and both are needed. Oracles, logia, are words, utterances of God (Romans 3:2). That is a weighty standard. Not that every Christian’s words are inspired, but that anyone speaking in the congregation, teaching, preaching, exhorting, should handle the responsibility as though delivering God’s own utterances: faithfully conveying his word, not their own opinions, carefully, and not casually (2 Timothy 4:2).

The strength that God supplies. Supplies, chorēgei, is the choregos word: in Athens a wealthy citizen funded a chorus for the great drama festivals and paid lavishly for everything it needed, costumes, training and all. The word came to mean provide abundantly. The servant does not run on his own reserves. Practical service, cooking, visiting, cleaning, giving, administering, depends on God’s strength, not ours, and God is a generous sponsor.

Through Jesus Christ. In everything, not only in the dramatic gifts. The gifts come from Christ: grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift, says Paul of the ascended Lord (Ephesians 4:7–8). They are shaped like Christ, who spoke only what the Father gave him to say (John 12:49) and came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45). And the glory returns through Christ, since our spiritual sacrifices are acceptable to God only through Jesus Christ (2:5). He is the way the gifts come down and the way the praise goes up.

Glory and dominion. This is why Peter breaks into doxology mid-letter. A man thinking about gifts rightly ends up talking about God rather than about gifts. Him may be God or Christ; the grammar allows either, and either way all glory is his. Dominion, kratos, is might, the power to rule. The scattered, powerless congregations are reminded that the one they serve holds all power for ever.

Does whoever speaks include prophecy and tongues today? Peter divides the gifts into speaking and serving, and the speaking he has in mind is the church’s teaching, preaching and exhortation, handled as God’s word, not new revelation. Continuationists (Christians who believe that all the gifts of the apostolic age continue today) include prophecy here, and they are brothers and sisters whose love for Christ we gladly recognise; the more likely reading is that those who speak in the church today speak as one who speaks oracles of God by faithfully passing on the words God has already given. The revelatory gifts served to lay the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20), and with the canon complete, Scripture is sufficient.

How do I find out what my gift is? Not mainly by taking a test, but by serving. Look at the needs around you in your church and start meeting them. Over time you will find what you do well, what others are blessed by, and what you find yourself drawn to. Ask mature Christians who know you what they see in you. Do not despise ordinary gifts: Peter puts serving beside speaking, and the person who stacks chairs, keeps accounts or visits the sick is as much a steward of God’s grace as the preacher. And remember that your gift is not your identity; it is God’s grace, lent to you, for others.

On a Tuesday. Before you serve someone this week, pray: Lord, supply the strength. Afterwards, say: to you be the glory. And if you have been holding back, waiting to be asked or to feel ready, step forward. The servant who buried his talent did so because he thought his master hard (Matthew 25:24–25); yours is the generous God who supplies.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last movement of the letter speaks as though the fire has already come. Peter tells his readers how to read it: as a share in Christ’s sufferings, a place where the Spirit of glory rests, and the start of God’s refining of his own house. It ends in trust in a faithful Creator.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgement Beginning at Home

Do not be surprised by the fiery trial. To suffer as a Christian is no shame; entrust your soul to a faithful Creator while doing good.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: “Christian” was probably an outsiders’ insult, and Peter told them to wear it.

Now: The name Christ gave us is worth bearing; let any suffering be for that name, not for wrongdoing or interfering.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, do not be surprised. Beloved, again: Peter never addresses suffering people coldly. The word for surprised, xenizesthe, think it strange, is the one used in verse 4 of the pagans, who were taken aback that Christians would not join them. Peter turns it round: they are astonished at you; do not you be astonished at this. The fiery trial, pyrōsis, is literally the burning: the word used of smelting metal in a furnace, and it reaches back to 1:7, where faith is refined like gold. Severe persecution is in view, and some think this anticipates Nero’s persecution of AD 64, when Christians in Rome were burned as living torches. In Asia Minor the fire was probably not yet literal, but the word was chosen with care: what felt like burning was the refiner’s furnace of 1:7.

To test you. When it comes, not if. And to test you, pros peirasmon, names the purpose, which is the whole point of the sentence. God uses the fire to refine faith (1:6–7). A trial with a purpose is a different experience from a trial without one, though the heat is identical.

Something strange. There is the pastoral target. The danger is not only the suffering but the interpretation: the conclusion that this is abnormal, that it means God has withdrawn, that other Christians somewhere are having an easier time and must be doing it better. Peter’s answer is that persecution is not a deviation from the Christian life but a normal feature of it. If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you (John 15:18–20; 2 Timothy 3:12). Which is a hard word and a strangely freeing one: a great deal of the pain of suffering is the suspicion that it should not be happening.

Insofar as you share. The measure is careful: insofar as. Peter is not commanding joy in suffering generally, but in the specific portion of it that is genuinely a share in Christ’s. And share, koinōneite, is the fellowship word: participate in, have communion in. This is participation, not imitation. Suffering for Christ is fellowship with him (Philippians 3:10; Colossians 1:24). Not adding to his atonement, which is complete, but sharing in the opposition the world gave him. The hostility aimed at him in Jerusalem is now aimed at his body in Bithynia, and when his people bear it, they are standing with him. Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4).

When his glory is revealed. The joy is not two joys but one, arriving in two instalments. What is begun now under the fire will be completed at the revelation, and the second verb is the exuberant one: be glad, agalliōmenoi, exult, the word for shouting gladness, leaping for joy (1:6, 8). Present joy in suffering leads to overflowing joy at his return. The pattern: suffering, then glory (1:11; Romans 8:17). Peter had seen it once already, on a high mountain, when the face of his Lord shone like the sun (Matthew 17:1–2; 2 Peter 1:16–18); and he knew the glory that was coming was real.

How can I rejoice when I am suffering? Not by pretending it does not hurt, but by looking past the pain to what it means and where it leads. You rejoice that you belong to Christ so truly that the world treats you as it treated him; that the Spirit rests on you (v. 14); that your faith is being refined; and that the glory coming is beyond all comparison (Romans 8:18). The apostles left the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41). You may weep and rejoice in the same hour. Joy here is not a feeling you produce, but a confidence God gives as you keep your eyes on Christ.

Should I expect persecution if I live faithfully? Yes, in some form, though its shape varies enormously. For some believers today it means prison, beatings, the loss of home or life; for others, mockery, exclusion, a career closed off, family rejection. Paul says all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted (2 Timothy 3:12). Do not seek it, and do not provoke it by foolishness (v. 15). But do not be surprised by it, and do not conclude that God has abandoned you when it comes. And pray for the persecuted church around the world, which is bearing the fiery trial in its full heat today.

verseByVerse.quote: If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Insulted for the name. Insulted, oneidizesthe, means reproached, reviled. For the name of Christ: because you bear his name and belong to him. Not for being difficult, or tactless, or socially awkward. Peter will make the distinction explicit in the very next verse, and he is careful never to let a Christian claim the blessing for trouble he brought on himself. And insult is the specific form named. Not imprisonment or death at this stage, but reviling, the ordinary daily contempt of neighbours. Which is what most Christians under pressure actually face, then and now: not a courtroom but a reputation quietly destroyed.

You are blessed. Blessed, makarioi: the Beatitude again, as in 3:14, echoing Jesus: blessed are you when others revile you and persecute you and utter all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account (Matthew 5:11–12). Peter keeps returning to a sermon he heard on a hillside.

The Spirit of glory. The Spirit of glory and of God is the Holy Spirit, who brings God’s glory with him. The verb rests, anapauetai, rests, abides, settles, is the one used in Isaiah 11:2, where the Spirit of the LORD rests on the shoot from the stump of Jesse: a messianic text. Peter says the same Spirit who rested on the Messiah settles on an insulted congregation in Bithynia. And there is very likely an echo of the glory cloud that rested on the tabernacle, when the glory of the LORD filled it and Moses could not enter (Exodus 40:34–35). The presence that filled the tent now rests on people being sworn at in the street. Like Stephen, whose face shone like the face of an angel as they gnashed their teeth at him, and who saw the glory of God (Acts 6:15; 7:55). Which inverts the whole appearance of things. The neighbours see a group whose reputation is in ruins. Peter says the visible shame is the outward face of an invisible glory, and that the Spirit is not merely with them despite the insults but is resting on them precisely there.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add: on their part he is blasphemed, but on your part he is glorified. The earliest manuscripts lack it, so most modern Bibles omit it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only persecuted believers have the Spirit. All believers have him (Romans 8:9). It means that in persecution the Spirit’s presence is specially manifest and real.

How can I know the Spirit is resting on me when I feel nothing but humiliation? Peter does not say you will feel it; he says it is so. The Spirit’s presence is a fact grounded in God’s promise, not a sensation you must manufacture. Often believers who have suffered for Christ look back and see it: a strength they did not have, a peace that made no sense, words that came when they needed them (Matthew 10:19–20), a love for their enemies they could not explain. In the moment, trust the promise. The insult is real, but so is the glory, and only one of them will last.

On a Tuesday. If you are mocked for Christ this week, at work, online, at a family meal, take heart: God’s glory rests on you. Say so to yourself, quietly, while it happens: the Spirit of glory is here. Then answer with gentleness, or with silence, but not with shame.

For worship. The Spirit who hovered over the waters of creation, who filled the tabernacle with glory, who rested on Jesus at the Jordan like a dove, now rests on the mocked and the slandered people of Christ. The world sees only their disgrace; heaven sees the glory cloud settled over them. He does not abandon his people in their humiliation; he chooses that very place to dwell. Glory to the Father who sends him, glory to the Son who poured him out, and glory to the Spirit who rests on the weakest saint as on a temple.

verseByVerse.quote: But let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler. Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not as a murderer. Peter will not let the blessing of verse 14 be claimed by a Christian who has earned his trouble. Suffering is only blessed if it is undeserved. The distinction has run through the letter (2:20; 3:17) and he states it once more, bluntly. Evildoer, kakopoios, is criminal, wrongdoer, the very accusation pagans were making against Christians (2:12). Do not prove them right.

Or as a meddler. Then the fourth item, and it does not belong with the first three. Meddler, allotriepiskopos, is found nowhere earlier in Greek literature, and Peter may have coined it. It means something like an overseer of other people’s business: a busybody. Set beside murder and theft it is startling, and the placing is the point. Peter puts interfering in other people’s affairs in a list with felonies, because in a small suspected minority the busybody does real damage. It may describe Christians who stirred up trouble by interfering in their neighbours’ lives, tactlessly condemning pagan customs, or causing unnecessary offence. A Christian who cannot keep out of his neighbours’ business will generate hostility and then mistake it for persecution.

As a Christian. The word Christian appears only three times in the New Testament (Acts 11:26; 26:28; and here), and this is the only place where a believer takes it up as a name to be worn. It was coined at Antioch (Acts 11:26) and was almost certainly an outsiders’ nickname: Christ-people, Christ-ites, partisans of Christ, perhaps used mockingly. Here it appears to be becoming a legal charge. Half a century later the governor Pliny asked the emperor whether Christians in Bithynia were to be punished for the name itself, even without any crime, and executed those who would not deny it.

Let him not be ashamed. Ashamed, aischynesthō. There is no shame in suffering for Christ: I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation (Romans 1:16; 2 Timothy 1:8, 12). So Peter takes the label the neighbours were using as an insult and tells them to wear it. That is what he means by not being ashamed: the name is being thrown at them, and the instruction is to catch it. And no one knew better than Peter what it was to be ashamed of the name. In a courtyard by a fire he had said, I do not know the man (Matthew 26:72).

Numbered with the transgressors. There is a reason Peter will not let a Christian suffer as an evildoer, and it is the cross. Christ was handed to Pilate with the words, if this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you (John 18:30). He was crucified between two robbers, and Jesus himself had said that the Scripture must be fulfilled in him: he was numbered with the transgressors (Luke 22:37; Isaiah 53:12). He bore the criminal’s name and the criminal’s death, though he committed no sin (2:22). He did it so that sinners could be called by his name instead. To be a Christian is to carry the name of the Anointed One, who took the evildoer’s place; to earn the evildoer’s sentence by our own misconduct would be to turn his substitution into a joke.

In that name. In that name, en tō onomati toutō: because he bears the name Christian. The shame is not merely to be endured but converted. The mockers supplied the word; the Christian is to make it an occasion of praise, which takes the sting out of an insult more completely than any denial could.

How do I tell the difference between being persecuted and being a nuisance? Ask honestly what the people opposing you are objecting to. Is it your faith in Christ, your refusal to sin, your honest witness? Or is it your tone, your tactlessness, your habit of correcting everyone, your neglect of your work, your political rage dressed in Christian language? Ask a wise friend, because we are poor judges of ourselves. If you find you have brought the trouble on yourself, apologise and change; that is not compromise but humility. If after honest examination the offence is Christ himself, then stand firm and rejoice.

Does this mean I should keep my faith private to avoid trouble? No. Peter tells them not to be ashamed of the name, and to be ready to give an account of their hope (3:15). Keeping out of other people’s business is not the same as keeping quiet about Christ. You can speak of him openly, kindly and without apology, while refusing to be a busybody who polices your neighbours’ lives. The aim is that if you are opposed, it will be for the name, and for nothing else.
verseByVerse.note: “Christian” was first a nickname given by outsiders; it appears only three times in the New Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God; and if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God? And "If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?" Therefore let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The household of God. A startling sentence, and it reframes everything the letter has described. Time, kairos, is the appointed season. Judgement, krima. Household of God, oikou tou theou, is the church, God’s temple and family (2:5; 1 Timothy 3:15). The idea is Ezekiel’s. When judgement fell on Jerusalem, the command to the executioners was: begin at my sanctuary (Ezekiel 9:6), God’s own house first. And Malachi foretold that the Lord would come suddenly to his temple and sit as a refiner, purifying the sons of Levi (Malachi 3:1–5). Peter is saying that the suffering these congregations are enduring is not merely persecution from outside; it is the first movement of God’s own sifting, and it begins with his people. For believers this judgement is the refining fire of suffering, purifying them (v. 12). That is not a comfortable thought and it is a clarifying one. Their trials are not outside God’s programme, and they are not evidence of his absence. He has started, and he has started at home.

And if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God? Outcome, telos, end. The argument runs from lesser to greater and Peter leaves it as a question, which is more forceful than a statement. If God’s refining is this painful for his own children, how terrible will his final judgement be for those who reject the gospel? They will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:8–9). The reader is left to do the arithmetic about his persecutors, which is a far more sobering thing than being told. And note the phrase: those who do not obey the gospel. The gospel is not only an offer but a summons, and to refuse it is disobedience.

And if the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner? Verse 18 quotes Proverbs 11:31 as it stands in the Greek Old Testament. Scarcely, molis, means with difficulty. Not that salvation is uncertain or only barely achieved, nor that the righteous are saved by a narrow margin or barely enough grace. It means saved with difficulty: through fire, through great trial and suffering, through the process this letter has been describing. Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22). Salvation is entirely secure, because God guards us (1:5), and the road to it is hard, and Peter has never pretended otherwise. If the righteous pass through such fire, what of the ungodly?

According to God’s will. Then the conclusion, and it gathers up the whole chapter. According to God’s will, kata to thelēma tou theou: suffering is not outside God’s control (3:17). Not one of these sufferings has slipped past him.

A faithful Creator. The verb entrust, paratithesthōsan, is the deposit word: commit, hand over for safekeeping, as one deposits valuables with a trusted friend before a journey. It is the word Jesus used on the cross: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! (Luke 23:46), echoing Psalm 31:5, where David prays: into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O LORD, faithful God. Peter takes both halves of that psalm verse, the committing and the faithful God, and puts them together. And the thought is the one used of Christ in 2:23, handing his case to the just Judge. The title chosen for God is exact: Creator, ktistēs, used of him nowhere else in the New Testament. A man handing over his soul is giving it back to the one who made it, and faithful, pistos, means the deposit will be there when he asks for it. The God who made you is faithful; he will care for what he made. Paul could say: I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me (2 Timothy 1:12).

While doing good. Doing good, en agathopoiia. The entrusting is done while doing good: not instead of acting, but in the middle of it. Trusting God does not mean passive resignation. The hand that commits the soul to God goes on working for the neighbour.

Is God punishing me through my suffering? Not in the sense of making you pay for your sins, which Christ has fully paid. There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). But God does discipline his children, out of love, to make them holy (Hebrews 12:6, 10), and he uses suffering to refine and purify. So the question to ask is not, what is God making me pay for? but, what is my Father teaching me, and how can I grow? Sometimes suffering exposes a sin to turn from; often it is simply the road all his children walk. Either way, it comes from a Father’s hand, not a Judge’s sentence.

How do I actually entrust my soul to God? By handing over, in prayer, the things you cannot control: your life, your future, your reputation, the outcome of the trial, the people who are hurting you. Say it to him plainly, as Jesus did: into your hands. Remind yourself of who he is: your Creator, who made you and knows you, and faithful, who has never broken a promise. Then go on doing the good in front of you. When anxiety returns, entrust again. It is not a single act but a lifelong habit, and the dying Christ shows its last and greatest form.

Does this verse teach that hell is real and eternal? It points to it. If even the righteous pass through refining fire, the end of those who do not obey the gospel is far worse, and Scripture describes that end as conscious, eternal punishment, away from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:9; Matthew 25:46). Peter does not dwell on it, and nor should we with relish. But he does not soften it either, because only the truth about judgement makes sense of the urgency of the gospel and the wonder of grace. The fire that the ungodly will face is the fire Christ endured in the place of all who trust him.

On a Tuesday. Pray Jesus’ words today: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit. Say them over the thing you are most anxious about. Then do one good thing for someone else, right away, while the trouble is still unresolved. And pray for someone you know who does not obey the gospel; the question of verse 17 is meant to move us to plead with God, and with them.
