5.title: Humble Yourselves: Elders, Community, and the God of All Grace
5.overview: The last chapter has three movements: elders are to shepherd God’s flock (vv. 1–5); the whole church is to humble itself under God’s mighty hand, cast its anxieties on him and resist the devil (vv. 6–11); and closing greetings place the letter in “Babylon”, almost certainly Rome (vv. 12–14). It closes with a benediction for suffering people: after a little while, the God of all grace will himself restore, confirm, strengthen and establish them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Shepherd the Flock of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter writes to the elders as a fellow elder, naming three temptations of leadership and the Chief Shepherd who is coming. Then he turns to the younger, and to everyone: put on humility, because God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble.
verseByVerse.theology:
Three Temptations and Their Remedies

Elders are to shepherd God’s flock willingly, eagerly and by example, not under compulsion, not for gain, not by domineering. The flock is not theirs, and its Owner is coming.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter wrote to elders as a fellow elder, not as an apostle.

Now: Everyone is to tie on the servant’s apron of humility.

verseByVerse.quote: So I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, as well as a partaker in the glory that is going to be revealed:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Peter 5 closes the letter with instructions for a suffering church. Peter, a fellow elder and witness of Christ’s sufferings, urges the elders to shepherd God’s flock willingly, eagerly and by example, not for money or by domineering; the Chief Shepherd will give them an unfading crown of glory (vv. 1–4). The younger submit to the elders, and all clothe themselves with humility, for God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble (v. 5). So humble yourselves under God’s mighty hand, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you (vv. 6–7). Be alert: the devil prowls like a roaring lion; resist him, firm in faith, with believers worldwide (vv. 8–9). After a little suffering the God of all grace will himself restore and establish you (vv. 10–11). The letter ends: this is the true grace of God, stand firm in it; greetings from Babylon and from Mark; peace (vv. 12–14).

So I exhort the elders. So, oun, therefore: because judgement begins at God’s household (4:17), its leaders must be faithful. Elders, presbyterous, plural: the leaders of each local church, also called overseers and shepherds (vv. 2–4; Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7). Every congregation Peter writes to has more than one, and he speaks to them first, because a suffering flock needs faithful shepherds more than anything.

As a fellow elder. Peter could have written as an apostle, and the letter opened that way (1:1). Addressing church leaders about how to lead, he sets the title down and takes the same chair they are sitting in. Fellow elder, sympresbyteros, appears nowhere else in the New Testament or in earlier Greek, so Peter may have coined it for this sentence: not authority over them but experience alongside them.

A witness. Witness, martys, the word that would come to mean martyr, because so many witnesses died for their testimony, Peter among them, as the early church remembered. Peter saw Jesus’ suffering firsthand: in Gethsemane, from the courtyard of the trial, where he failed, and perhaps from a distance at the cross. When he tells elders to shepherd the flock, the words come from a man who had denied he knew the Shepherd at all, and been given the sheep anyway.

A partaker in the glory. Look at the tenses. He was a witness of the sufferings; he is a partaker of a glory not yet revealed. Peter puts himself and them in the same position, between a suffering already seen and a glory still coming, which is where this whole letter has located its readers (4:13). And there may be a memory in the word. Peter had seen glory revealed once, on the mountain, when the Lord’s face shone like the sun (Matthew 17:1–8; 2 Peter 1:16–18), and had wanted to build shelters and stay. He writes now as a man who knows the glory is real and that it is not yet time.

Where Christians differ: was Peter the first pope? Roman Catholic teaching holds that Christ made Peter head of the universal church, with authority passed to the bishops of Rome as his successors, reading Matthew 16:18–19 as founding a continuing office. Many devout Catholics hold this sincerely and love Christ; this commentary differs from them here with respect, because of what the texts themselves say. This commentary’s view: Peter calls himself a fellow elder, not a supreme pontiff. Christ is the Chief Shepherd (v. 4), the cornerstone (2:6), and the head of the church (Ephesians 1:22; Colossians 1:18). Peter was a leading apostle, the one God used to open the door of the gospel to Jews at Pentecost and to Gentiles at Cornelius’ house (Acts 2; 10), but the foundation of the church is the apostles and prophets together, with Christ as cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20), and Paul could rebuke Peter publicly (Galatians 2:11–14). The New Testament knows nothing of a papacy or of Peter’s authority being passed to Roman bishops. Local churches are led by a plurality of elders, under Christ.

Does Peter’s calling himself a fellow elder tell against the papacy? Roman Catholic teaching sees Peter as the first bishop of Rome with authority over the whole church (compare Matthew 16:18–19). Here Peter, writing probably from Rome (v. 13), places himself alongside the elders, not over them, and points them to Christ, the chief Shepherd. Nothing in his letters claims a supreme office or successors. Christians who order their churches differently, under bishops or under congregational rule, still agree that every church leader answers to the one Chief Shepherd.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for the elders of your church, one by one, and ask God to keep them humble, faithful and unafraid. If you are an elder, sit for a moment where Peter sat, between the sufferings you have seen and the glory you have not.

For worship. Peter saw him suffer, and Peter saw him shine. The face that was spat on in the high priest’s courtyard was the face that blazed like the sun on the mountain, and both are the face of our Lord. Every under-shepherd of his flock, from Peter in Rome to the faithful elder in the smallest chapel, will one day stand in the glory he has promised to share.

verseByVerse.quote: shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you; not for shameful gain, but eagerly; not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shepherd the flock of God. Shepherd, poimanate: tend, feed, care for as a shepherd. It is the command Jesus gave Peter: tend my sheep (John 21:16), and now Peter passes it on. Shepherding includes feeding (teaching the word), leading, protecting from wolves, seeking the lost, binding up the injured and caring for the weak (Ezekiel 34:1–16). Peter has already given the titles of shepherd and overseer to Christ (2:25), which fixes the terms: these men are under-shepherds, and the flock is not theirs. It belongs to God, and the elder is among it rather than above it. And it belongs to God because it was bought: Paul told the Ephesian elders to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood (Acts 20:28). Every elder handles sheep that cost the Son of God his life.

Exercising oversight. Episkopountes, overseeing, watching over: the word bishop comes from it. Here, as in Acts 20:17, 28 and Titus 1:5–7, elders and overseers appear to be the same office. Then three pairs follow, each a temptation and its remedy, and together they search a leader’s motives as closely as any passage in Scripture.

Willingly. Under compulsion, anankastōs, means reluctantly, because they must. The first danger is doing it from duty, or because nobody else will, or because you cannot see how to stop. In a persecuted church, being an elder made you a target, and the temptation to serve reluctantly was real. As God would have you, kata theon, locates the willingness: not natural enthusiasm but a work taken up under God, from a heart that loves him and his people. The KJV lacks this phrase, following later manuscripts; several early ones have it, so most modern Bibles include it.

Not for shameful gain. Aischrokerdōs, in greed for shameful profit; the related adjective appears in 1 Timothy 3:8 and Titus 1:7. Peter assumes elders could profit from the work, through the church’s support or through handling its funds, or the warning would be pointless. Elders may be paid (1 Timothy 5:17–18), but money must not be the motive. The alternative, prothymōs, eagerly, wholeheartedly, is the opposite of a man calculating what the post returns.

Not domineering. The third is power, and it has ruined many. Domineering, katakyrieuontes, is the very word the Lord used when he said the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, but it shall not be so among you (Mark 10:42–43). Peter was there. He was among the ten who were indignant when James and John asked for the best seats, and he heard the Lord finish the sentence: even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). The model for an elder is not the Gentile ruler but the ransoming Christ. Those in your charge, tōn klērōn, are the allotted ones: the people entrusted to each elder as a share is allotted, not owned.

But being examples. Examples, typoi, are patterns, the mark left by a seal (1 Timothy 4:12; Titus 2:7). Shepherds in Jesus’ world usually led their flocks rather than driving them from behind, and the sheep followed the voice they knew (John 10:4). And the alternative is not weak leadership but a costlier kind. A man who leads by command need only be obeyed; a man who leads by example has to be worth copying. No elder meets that standard without fault; the Chief Shepherd met it perfectly in his place, and that is why a failing shepherd can confess, be forgiven and go on.

What it does not mean. Not domineering does not mean elders have no authority. They lead and must be obeyed (v. 5; Hebrews 13:17). It means their authority is exercised humbly, by example, for the flock’s good.

What should a church member do if an elder is domineering or abusive? Speak to him first if it is safe, honestly and respectfully, as you would any brother (Matthew 18:15). If that fails or the matter is serious, take it to the other elders, who share responsibility for oversight; this is one reason the New Testament gives churches a plurality of elders. Paul says a charge against an elder should be received on the evidence of two or three witnesses, and that those who persist in sin should be rebuked publicly (1 Timothy 5:19–20). If there is abuse or a crime, it must be reported to the authorities. Elders are under-shepherds, not owners, and they answer to Christ and to the church.

On a Tuesday. The Shepherd who laid down his life for you now lives in you by his Spirit, so whatever leadership you have, in a home, a group or a workplace, ask which of Peter’s three temptations is closest to you: reluctance, money or power. Then, asking him for the gladness you lack, do the opposite once. And if you are not a leader, make your elders’ work a joy (Hebrews 13:17): thank one of them this week.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the chief Shepherd appears. Chief Shepherd, archipoimēn: Jesus Christ (2:25; John 10:11; Hebrews 13:20). The word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and it settles the whole passage. There is one Chief Shepherd, and every elder is under him. Appears, phanerōthentos, is revealed: at his return. It also answers the three temptations of the previous verse at their root. A man who believes the flock belongs to someone else, who is coming back, will not serve grudgingly, or for money, or by domineering, because none of those makes sense if you are minding somebody else’s sheep and he is due home.

The unfading crown of glory. The crown is stephanos, the victor’s wreath at the games rather than a royal diadem: a circle of leaves, olive at Olympia, pine at the Isthmian games near Corinth, celery at Nemea, and everyone watching knew how quickly it browned. So Peter’s adjective is chosen with care. Unfading, amarantinos, is from the amaranth, the flower the ancients used as a symbol of what does not wither; he used the same root of the inheritance in 1:4. The wreath handed to an athlete was dead within the week; this one is made of something else (1 Corinthians 9:25; 2 Timothy 4:8). The crown of glory most likely means the crown that consists of glory, as the crown of life in James 1:12 means the crown which is life. The reward is not a decoration to wear but a share in the glory Peter has just said he is a partaker of.

A reward for the unseen. That is a striking thing to promise elders in a persecuted network of house churches. Their work was often unpaid or barely paid, unnoticed outside their own street, and dangerous. Peter tells them the recognition is coming from the only person whose opinion is final.

Is it right to serve God for a reward? Yes, if the reward is what God offers and the motive is love for him. Scripture repeatedly holds out reward as an encouragement (Matthew 6:4; Hebrews 11:6), and Jesus himself endured the cross for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). What is wrong is serving for the wrong reward: money, praise, power, the admiration of the congregation. The crown of glory is not wages that put God in our debt; it is a gift of grace crowning the work grace produced. And the faithful will cast their crowns before the throne (Revelation 4:10), because the best part of the reward is the one who gives it.

On a Tuesday. If you serve faithfully without recognition, in the crèche, at the door, in the hospital visit nobody hears about, the Chief Shepherd sees, and he will reward. When you are tempted to resent being overlooked, remember whose wreath you are working for.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, you who are younger, be subject to the elders. Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another, for "God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, you who are younger. Having addressed the leaders, Peter turns to those most likely to chafe under them. Younger, neōteroi: younger people in the church, or perhaps a group of younger men who served the church practically, like the young men who carried out Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:6, 10). Elders here may mean the office or simply older people; probably the office, continuing from verses 1–4. Be subject, hypotagēte, is the same word as 2:13, 18; 3:1: the posture the letter has asked of citizens, slaves and wives.

Clothe yourselves with humility. Then the scope widens: all of you. Humility is for everyone, not just the young, and it is towards one another, elders to members as much as members to elders. The verb, enkombōsasthe, is unusual and vivid. It means to tie something on, and a related noun was used of an apron tied over one’s clothes for work. Peter is telling the whole congregation to put on a servant’s apron. And it is hard not to think he had seen it happen. In the upper room the Lord rose from supper, tied a towel round himself, and washed their feet, and Peter had objected, loudly, and been told: if I do not wash you, you have no share with me (John 13:4–17). The picture he reaches for here is one he originally refused.

God opposes the proud. The quotation is Proverbs 3:34 in its Greek form, and James uses it too (James 4:6): evidently a text the early church leaned on hard. The word for opposes, antitassetai, is military: to draw up in battle order against. God does not merely decline to help the proud; he takes the field opposite them. And grace, being a gift, can only be received by open hands, which is why humility is not one virtue among several here but the posture in which anything at all can be received. God pours grace on the humble as water runs to the lowest place.

What does humility actually look like? It looks like being willing to do the lowly job without being asked or thanked; listening more than speaking; admitting when you are wrong, quickly and without excuses; rejoicing when others are praised; asking for help; receiving correction without sulking; and thinking of yourself less, rather than thinking less of yourself. It is not putting yourself down, refusing compliments, or pretending you have no gifts. C. S. Lewis remarked that the humble man will not be thinking about humility at all, because he will not be thinking about himself. The root of it is seeing yourself rightly before God: a sinner saved by grace, with nothing you did not receive (1 Corinthians 4:7).

I am young and disagree with my church leaders. What should I do? Respect them, pray for them, and speak to them. Submission does not mean you must have no opinions, or that elders are never wrong. It means you approach them with humility rather than contempt, assume the best of their motives, ask questions before making accusations, and support their decisions where conscience allows, even when you would have done it differently. If a matter is serious, raise it privately and respectfully. Do not stir up a faction. And be willing to consider that age and experience may see what you do not yet see, just as you may see what they have missed.

On a Tuesday. The Lord tied on the towel and washed you first. When you are corrected this week, by a spouse, a boss, an elder or a child, try saying thank you before you say but.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — Cast Your Anxieties, and Stand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole church is to humble itself under God’s hand, handing him its worries, and to stay alert against an enemy who hunts the isolated. Suffering is for a little while; the God of all grace will himself restore his people. Peter then sums up his letter as the true grace of God and closes with greetings from “Babylon”, Rome.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why Worry Is Treated as Pride

Humble yourselves by casting all your anxieties on God, because he cares for you. After a little while, the God of all grace will himself restore you.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The devil prowled like a roaring lion, looking for anyone cut off from the flock.

Now: Resist him, firm in the faith, knowing the same sufferings are shared by believers throughout the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Under the mighty hand of God. The therefore follows the proverb: since that is how God deals with pride and humility, put yourself on the right side of it. Humble yourselves, tapeinōthēte, is passive in form: be humbled, accept the humbling. The mighty hand of God is an exodus phrase: God brought Israel out of Egypt with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm (Exodus 3:19; 6:1; Deuteronomy 9:26). It is also his hand in disciplining them. The hand is heavy; it is also the hand that delivers. Accept God’s dealings with you, including suffering, without resentment or resistance.

At the proper time. En kairō, in due season: God’s timing, not ours. The lifting is his work and his timing. A man who insists on being raised now has taken the job out of the right hands.

Under the mighty hand, to the right hand. Christ walked this verse first. He humbled himself to the point of death, and therefore God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:8–9). In Gethsemane he did not hide his anguish; he offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to the one who was able to save him (Hebrews 5:7), and then went under the mighty hand to the cross. At the proper time God lifted him, as Peter preached at Pentecost: exalted at the right hand of God (Acts 2:33). The road Peter commends to anxious believers runs from that garden to that throne, and they walk it in him.

Casting all your anxieties on him. The grammar matters. Casting is not a separate command; it is a participle attached to humble yourselves: the casting is how the humbling is done. We do not usually think of worry as pride. Peter sees a link: holding on to your anxieties can be a way of insisting that the situation is yours to manage, and handing them over is an act of self-lowering. This is not a rebuke to the anxious. Peter writes to frightened people, and he ends the sentence with he cares for you, so the call to humility comes as an open door, not a scolding. Casting, epiripsantes, is a decisive verb: throw it, the word used of the disciples flinging their cloaks on the colt for Jesus to ride (Luke 19:35). It echoes Psalm 55:22: cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you. And all leaves no category too small to bother him with. Anxieties, merimna, is the word Jesus used when he said do not be anxious about your life (Matthew 6:25–34).

Because he cares for you. The ground of the whole thing is not that he is capable but that he is concerned. The word, melei, means it matters to him. There is a play of sound in Greek between our merimna and his melei: our care, his care. Peter is writing to people whose neighbours had decided they were nothing, and the last word of the sentence is that they are on somebody’s mind. The God who keeps the stars in their courses has you in his thoughts, by name.

Is anxiety a sin? This verse is an invitation, not a rebuke: he cares for you. Some anxiety comes from pride and self-reliance, and needs to be cast on God in humility (v. 6). But some anxiety has bodily causes and is an illness, and seeking help from a doctor or counsellor, or taking medication, is no lack of faith. Bring the burden to God, again and again, and use every means he provides.

How do I actually cast my worries on God? Specifically and repeatedly. Name each worry to him in prayer, one by one, out loud or on paper: not a vague request for peace, but this diagnosis, this debt, this child, this meeting. Tell him what you fear will happen. Then deliberately hand it over: Father, this is yours; I cannot carry it. Do what is yours to do about it, and leave the rest. When the worry comes back, and it will, cast it again, without scolding yourself. Pair it with thanksgiving (Philippians 4:6–7), which reminds the heart of how often he has carried you before.

For worship. The hand that is mighty enough to part the sea is gentle enough to take our smallest care. He does not sigh when we come with the same worry for the hundredth time. He carried the whole weight of our sin on the cross, and he is not going to drop the lesser burdens now.

verseByVerse.quote: Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be sober-minded; be watchful. Two sharp imperatives, and the first has appeared before (1:13; 4:7): a clear head. The second, grēgorēsate, stay awake, is the word from Gethsemane: watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation (Matthew 26:41; Mark 14:37–38). Peter did neither, and slept, and within hours had denied his Lord three times (Mark 14:66–72). He is not issuing a command he has never failed. He knows the cost of not being watchful.

Your adversary the devil. Adversary, antidikos, is a courtroom word: the opponent in a lawsuit, the prosecutor. Devil, diabolos, means slanderer. That is a precise description of what these readers were experiencing: they were being accused, publicly and continuously. Satan accuses believers before God (Job 1–2; Zechariah 3:1; Revelation 12:10) and slanders them through human persecutors. He is real, personal and hostile.

Is belief in a personal devil not a relic of a superstitious age? It would be if the Bible pictured him as a horned figure behind every misfortune, but it does not. Scripture speaks of him soberly: a created being, a fallen angel, powerful but limited, already defeated, and working mostly through lies, accusation and fear (John 8:44). Many thoughtful people who have looked hard at the cruelty of the last century have found it difficult to explain by human weakness alone. And the denial suits him. A soldier who does not believe there is an enemy will not keep watch, which is exactly why Peter’s first words are be sober-minded; be watchful. The devil is not to be feared as God’s equal. He is to be taken seriously as God’s defeated rebel.

Like a roaring lion. Prowls, peripatei, walks about. The picture is hunting. In Scripture the lion’s roar is the sound of a terrifying enemy (Psalm 22:13; Ezekiel 22:25), and Peter’s point seems to be that this enemy works first on the nerves. The noise is a weapon, meant to frighten before it wounds. Under Nero, within a few years, Christians in Rome were sewn into the skins of wild beasts and torn by dogs, and in later persecutions they were literally thrown to lions.

Seeking someone to devour. Devour, katapiein, swallow up. The hunt is selective. He is looking for the one that has drifted from the group, the isolated, the weak, the careless, which is exactly what persecution does to a congregation.

Resist him, firm in your faith. Resist, antistēte, stand against, as in James 4:7: resist the devil, and he will flee from you. The command is to stand, not to attack. Firm, stereoi, is a solid word: settled, not moving, like a rock, the opposite of the scattering the roar is designed to produce. Resistance comes through faith, taking up the shield of faith (Ephesians 6:16), in the power of the Spirit rather than our own strength.

Sifted like wheat. Peter had been hunted before, and he knew who kept him. On the night of the betrayal Jesus said, Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail (Luke 22:31–32). The lion found him by a charcoal fire, and he fell; but his faith did not fail, because Christ had prayed for it. So when Peter says resist, firm in your faith, the firmness is not the believer’s own grip. It is the faith Christ prays for, held by the Lord who answered the devil in the wilderness with the word of God (Matthew 4:1–11) and disarmed him at the cross (Colossians 2:15).

Your brotherhood throughout the world. Brotherhood, adelphotēs, as in 2:17. Not a promise of relief but of company. Isolation is the lion’s method, and the answer is the knowledge that you are one of many, which is why Peter wrote a circular letter to churches across five regions rather than a private note.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every difficulty is a direct satanic attack, or that we should be obsessed with the devil. He is a defeated enemy (3:22; Colossians 2:15).

How does the devil actually attack Christians today? Mostly not with dramatic manifestations, but with the same tactics Peter names: accusation, fear and isolation. He accuses, telling you that you are too sinful for God to forgive, or that your faith is fake. He frightens, making obedience look too costly. He isolates, drawing you away from church and Christian friends until you are alone. He also deceives, with false teaching and with temptations dressed as freedom. The answer is the same as Peter’s: stay awake, stay in the word, stay with the flock, and when he accuses, answer with the blood of Christ. He is a lion, but he is a lion on a chain.

verseByVerse.quote: And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you. To him be the dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After you have suffered a little while. Peter does not remove the suffering from the sentence. It stands, and it is bounded. A little while, oligon, is the same phrase as 1:6, measured against the eternal glory in the next clause (2 Corinthians 4:17).

The God of all grace. The title is chosen for the moment. Not the God of all power, though he is; the God of all grace. Grace is God’s undeserved favour, his goodness given freely to people who have earned the opposite, and God is the source of every kind of it: saving grace, sustaining grace, strengthening grace, the many-coloured grace of 4:10. My grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:9).

To his eternal glory in Christ. Called, kalesas: God’s effectual call, the call that does not merely invite but actually brings a person to faith (1:15; 2:9, 21; 3:9). The calling looks past the suffering to the destination, his own glory (Romans 8:30), the glory Peter said in verse 1 he is a partaker of. And in Christ gives the road its shape. The prophets foretold the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories (1:11), and the risen Lord asked, was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? (Luke 24:26). Suffering, then glory, is first his story, and union with him makes it ours: we suffer a little while because he suffered once, and we will be glorified because he already is.

Restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish. Four verbs, piled up for assurance, and the emphatic word is himself, autos: God personally. Restore, katartisei, is the mending word: used of setting a broken bone and of repairing nets, which Peter had done for a living. When Jesus first called James and John they were in their boat mending their nets (Mark 1:19), the same verb. It assumes damage: the suffering will break something, and God will set it. Confirm, stērixei, to make firm, set fast, is the word the Lord used when he told Peter: when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers (Luke 22:32), and here Peter does just that. Strengthen, sthenōsei, is to fill with strength. And establish, themeliōsei, is to lay on a foundation so it cannot be shifted. This is what is called the perseverance of the saints, the teaching that those God truly calls he keeps to the end: God will finish what he started (Philippians 1:6). And it comes from a man who had been broken and repaired by name.

To him be the dominion. Dominion, kratos, power, might. The KJV reads glory and dominion, following later manuscripts that add glory; the earliest have dominion alone. Peter has just named the prowling lion; he ends by saying whose the dominion actually is. The devil roars, but God rules.

In the flow. Peter’s closing benediction comes here, before the greetings, and almost every word in it has appeared before. A little while recalls 1:6; called recalls 1:15 and 2:9; grace runs from 1:2 to 4:10; eternal glory in Christ gathers up the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories (1:11). Peter ends his teaching where he began it, in 1:3–5, with God himself keeping his people through trial to the end. Everything between, the submission, the slander, the fiery trial and the prowling lion, has been set inside these two promises.

What it does not mean. It does not promise that suffering will end in this life. Restoration may be partial now and complete in glory. But it is certain.

What if I feel broken beyond repair? Then this verse was written for you. Peter promises that God will restore, and the word assumes real damage: a broken bone, a torn net. He does not say the breaking did not happen or did not matter. He says God himself will mend it. That mending may begin now, slowly, through his word, his people, prayer and time, and sometimes through doctors and counsellors he provides; and it will be complete when Christ appears. Peter had been broken by his own denial, and Christ restored him on a beach. The God of all grace has never yet met a soul too broken for him.

On a Tuesday. Pray this promise back to God in the first person, naming the broken thing: you yourself will restore, confirm, strengthen and establish me. Then look for one person in your church who is broken by suffering, and be one of the hands God uses to strengthen them, as Peter was told to strengthen his brothers.

verseByVerse.quote: By Silvanus, a faithful brother as I regard him, I have written briefly to you, exhorting and declaring that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it. She who is at Babylon, who is likewise chosen, sends you greetings, and so does Mark, my son. Greet one another with the kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By Silvanus. Silvanus is the Silas of Acts, Paul’s companion on the second missionary journey, who sang hymns with him at midnight in the jail at Philippi (Acts 15:40; 16:19–25; 1 Thessalonians 1:1), a Roman citizen (Acts 16:37), and now carrying Peter’s letter. By, dia, through: he may have been Peter’s secretary, helping with the polished Greek of a Galilean fisherman, or the bearer of the letter, or both. That Paul’s companion helps Peter shows that the apostles were not rival parties.

I have written briefly. Five chapters, and a lifetime of experience compressed into them (compare Hebrews 13:22).

The true grace of God. That is Peter’s own summary of what he has written. After five chapters on suffering, submission and slander, he calls the whole thing grace: not advice, not endurance training, but true grace, alēthē charin. Suffering does not mean grace has failed; it is part of God’s true grace. And the grace has a name. The prophets, Peter wrote, spoke of the grace that was to be yours as they searched out the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow (1:10–11). The true grace of God is Christ himself, crucified and glorified, given to exiles.

Stand firm in it. The KJV reads wherein ye stand, a statement rather than a command, following later manuscripts; the earliest have the command. Peter does not say produce it, or earn it, or even fully understand it. Stand in it, as a man stands on solid ground in an earthquake.

She who is at Babylon. She is almost certainly the church there, God’s chosen lady (2 John 1), and Babylon is very probably a code name for Rome, as in Revelation 14:8; 17:5; 18:2, not the Mesopotamian city, which was largely deserted by then. Jewish writers after AD 70 used the name for Rome, which had destroyed Jerusalem as Babylon had in 586 BC; Peter, writing earlier, already sees Rome as the great pagan power and the city of exile. Early tradition places Peter in Rome at the end of his life, where he was martyred under Nero. Peter writes to exiles from the empire’s capital and calls it Babylon, reminding them that the church at the centre of the world is as much in a foreign country as the church in Bithynia. And likewise chosen, syneklektē, chosen together with you, hands them back the word he opened with (1:1).

And so does Mark, my son. John Mark, who abandoned Paul and Barnabas on the first missionary journey (Acts 13:13), was the cause of their sharp disagreement, and was later restored, so that Paul could call him very useful to me for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11). My son is affection, not paternity. Peter had gone to Mark’s mother’s house in Jerusalem when the angel freed him from prison, and found the church praying there (Acts 12:12). Early tradition, from Papias, says that Mark became Peter’s interpreter and wrote down in his Gospel what Peter preached. Two men who had both failed, both been restored, standing together at the end.

The kiss of love. The customary greeting among family members, used in the early church as a sign of family affection (Romans 16:16; 1 Corinthians 16:20). Slave and master, Jew and Gentile, greeting each other as brother and sister. The letter that has spoken so much of hostility ends with an instruction to touch each other.

Peace to all of you who are in Christ. Peace, eirēnē, the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, everything as it should be, offered to people who had very little of it, from a man who would shortly die in the city he calls Babylon. It was the first word the risen Lord spoke to the disciples gathered in the locked room: peace be with you (John 20:19). Peter ends where his Lord began.

Must Christians greet each other with a kiss today? The point is warm, holy affection between brothers and sisters, expressed in the form one’s culture uses. Where a kiss carries that meaning it may be used; elsewhere a handshake or an embrace obeys the command. The form may vary by culture; the warmth should not.

What does it mean to stand firm in grace? It means refusing to move off the ground God has put you on. Do not slide into earning your standing by performance, as though suffering meant you had not done enough. Do not slide into despair, as though suffering meant grace had failed. Do not slide into compromise, as though grace could be kept while denying Christ. Stand on what this letter has told you: you are chosen, born again, ransomed, guarded, loved, called to glory. Keep coming back to it in the word, at the Lord’s Table, among his people. Grace is not only how you began; it is where you stand every day until he comes.

On a Tuesday. Read 1 Peter through in one sitting this week; it takes about twenty minutes. Then write one sentence on what the true grace of God means for your life right now.

For worship. This is the true grace of God: that the Father chose exiles, the Spirit set them apart, the Son ransomed them with his blood; that he caused them to be born again to a living hope, guarded them by his power, refined them in the fire, and called them to his eternal glory. It is grace from the first verse to the last, grace that holds in Babylon and Bithynia, grace that turned a denier into an apostle and a deserter into an evangelist. And over every scattered, slandered, suffering child of God, the last word is his: peace, in Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Silvanus is the Silas of Acts. “Babylon” is very probably a code name for Rome. Mark is John Mark, whom early tradition links with Peter as the source of Mark’s Gospel.
